docs.text: # The Growing Calendar Where You Live Every seed packet asks you the same question, and it is always the same question: when do I start this. Nobody can answer it for you from a zone map or a national chart, because the answer is arithmetic done on three numbers that belong to your own ground. Those numbers are the date your spring frosts stop, the date your autumn frosts start, and how much daylight you get in between. Get those three, and every planting date you will ever need falls out of them by counting. This guide teaches the counting. Silverdale, Washington is the worked example throughout, because there is a real, sourced climate file behind it, but the method is the point and the method is the same everywhere. Swap in your own three numbers at the end and redo the sums. Two companion guides sit either side of this one. [Starting Seeds](/library#starting-seeds) is how to raise a transplant once you know when to sow it. [Your First Tomato](/library#your-first-tomato) is how to grow the plant once it is in the ground. This guide is only about when. ## The number most people plant to is a coin flip Here is the single most valuable idea in this document, and it is worth reading twice. **The average last frost date is not a deadline. It is a coin flip.** It is the 50th percentile: the date by which the last spring frost has finished in half of all years. In the other half of years, frost comes after it. Plant a tomato on your average last frost date every year for a decade and, on the long-run odds, you lose the plant in five of those ten years. Silverdale's average last spring frost is **March 29**. Its 90th-percentile date is **April 24**, and that is the useful one: past April 24, only about one year in ten still delivers a frost. The average is the date nearly every planting chart prints. The 90th-percentile date is the one you plant to. Here is the same idea as a table, for both ends of the year. | Last spring frost, 32 F | Date | Read it as | |---|---|---| | Earliest tenth of years | March 5 | Spring frost is finished by now in 1 year in 10 | | Median | March 29 | Finished by now in half of years, still coming in the other half | | Latest tenth | April 24 | Finished by now in 9 years in 10 | | First autumn frost, 32 F | Date | Read it as | |---|---|---| | Earliest tenth of years | October 26 | Frost has already hit by now in 1 year in 10 | | Median | November 14 | Has hit by now in half of years | | Latest tenth | December 1 | Has hit by now in 9 years in 10 | Both tables use the same rule, applied to opposite ends of the season. In spring you want the LATE date, because you are waiting for a danger to finish. In autumn you want the EARLY date, because you are racing a danger that is coming. Using the average at either end is betting your crop on a coin. So on the autumn side, October 26 is when your row cover needs to exist and be reachable in the dark. Not November 14. ## Two thresholds, and why 32 F is the optimistic one All the dates above are measured at 32 F, the freezing point of water, which is the threshold weather services publish. It is not the threshold your seedlings experience. Official air temperature is measured in a shaded, ventilated instrument shelter about head height above the ground. On a clear, calm night, the ground and everything lying on it radiate heat to the open sky and get colder than that shelter does, while cold air, being dense, drains downhill and pools in low ground. A reading of 36 F at the station can be a frozen seedling at soil level. NOAA publishes a 36 F threshold for exactly this reason, and for Silverdale it moves the calendar a long way: | Threshold | Spring date, 1-in-10 risk | Autumn counterpart | |---|---|---| | 32 F | April 24 | October 26 | | 36 F | May 13 | October 4 | **May 13 is six weeks later than the March 29 average.** That gap is the whole reason people lose tomatoes in May and blame themselves. Now the three season lengths, which are the same climate described three ways: | Measured how | Length | |---|---| | Growing season as NOAA publishes it (32 F, 50th percentile) | 227 days | | April 24 to October 26 (32 F, one-in-ten risk at each end) | 185 days | | May 13 to October 4 (36 F, one-in-ten risk at each end) | 144 days | The headline number is 227 days. The season you can plant frost-tender crops into without gambling is 144. Plan to 227 and your autumn tomatoes are a hope, not a plan. In practice most growers work between the two middle dates: put tender crops out from about April 24 with cover ready and used, or from about May 13 with nothing. Both are defensible. Planting to March 29 is not. ## Counting backwards: the spring side You now have an anchor date. Everything else is subtraction. There are only two shapes of crop, and they count differently. **Transplanted crops** (tomato, pepper, eggplant, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, melons) are raised indoors and moved out. The anchor is the plant-out date, and you subtract the indoor weeks to find the sowing date. **Direct-sown crops** (beans, carrots, peas, radish, lettuce, spinach, squash, corn) go into the ground as seed. Their anchor is not a frost date at all. It is the day your soil reaches the temperature that crop will germinate at, which is a different section below. The general arithmetic, which is what you take away from this guide: ``` Transplanted crop: sow indoors = plant-out date minus weeks indoors plant out = your chosen frost-risk date first harvest = plant-out date plus days to maturity Direct-sown crop: sow = the day your soil reaches the crop's minimum first harvest = sowing date plus days to maturity ``` The indoor weeks per crop are listed in [Starting Seeds](/library#starting-seeds) and are not repeated here. ## What "days to maturity" actually measures This is the step where most people's arithmetic quietly goes wrong, because the number on the packet does not mean what it looks like it means. For a set of crops it is counted **from the day you transplant**, not from the day you sowed the seed. Maryland Extension names that set: tomatoes, peppers, eggplants, muskmelons, watermelons, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower and Brussels sprouts. For every other annual crop the number counts from direct seeding. So a tomato packet reading "75 days" does not mean 75 days from the day you sowed. It means 75 days after the transplant went into the ground, and the six weeks you spent raising that transplant sit in front of it and are not in the number at all. Real elapsed time from seed is closer to 120 days. Two sourced anchors to calibrate against: Maryland Extension gives tomatoes 65 to 90 days from transplant, and sweet and hot peppers 70 to 85 days from transplanting, with bell peppers reaching mature green at 70 to 80 days and needing a further 2 to 3 weeks to colour up. Utah State notes that a transplanted tomato matures roughly four weeks before a tomato direct-seeded on the same ground, which is exactly the head start you bought with the indoor weeks. When a packet does not say which way it counts, assume transplanted crops count from transplant and everything else counts from sowing. ## Soil temperature is what actually governs germination A seed does not know the air temperature. It knows the temperature of the soil touching it. This is why planting by the calendar fails in a cold spring and why a warm week in March does not mean anything. Below its minimum, a seed does not germinate slowly. It sits, absorbs water, and rots. Maryland Extension is blunt about the common casualties: beans, cucumbers and melons need soil of at least 60 F to germinate. A selection from the germination table published by university extension services, in Fahrenheit: | Crop | Minimum soil temp | Optimum | |---|---|---| | Lettuce | 35 | 75 | | Onion | 35 | 75 | | Spinach | 35 | 70 | | Beet | 40 | 85 | | Cabbage | 40 | 85 | | Carrot | 40 | 80 | | Pea | 40 | 75 | | Radish | 40 | 85 | | Corn | 50 | 95 | | Tomato | 50 | 85 | | Bean, snap | 60 | 80 | | Cucumber | 60 | 95 | | Pepper | 60 | 85 | | Squash | 60 | 95 | Read the minimum column as "will eventually come up" and the optimum column as "comes up fast and evenly." The gap between them is large and it is where most germination disappointment lives. Lettuce sown at 40 F does germinate; it just takes weeks, and weeks in cold wet soil is plenty of time for something else to eat it. The tool is a soil thermometer, pushed to seed depth, read in the morning before the sun has warmed the surface, on several consecutive days rather than one. **Rule of thumb:** soil lags air by weeks, and it lags most where the ground is wet, shaded, north-facing or heavy, which describes a great deal of Silverdale. Half the land here is Alderwood, a thin gravelly mantle over dense glacial till that stays saturated through the wet season (see the [Silverdale gazetteer](/library#silverdale-wa) for the soils). Wet soil warms slowly, because the water has to be heated too. Do not guess this number. Measure it. It is the cheapest instrument in gardening and it settles arguments the calendar cannot. ## Day length: the limit that does not care how warm the afternoon was Temperature is the limit everyone watches. Daylight is the limit that quietly decides what is possible, and it is completely immune to weather. A February warm spell changes the temperature. It does not change the fact that February has February's light. Silverdale runs from 8.4 hours of daylight in midwinter to 16.0 hours at midsummer, a swing of nearly eight hours: | Month | Daylight | Month | Daylight | |---|---|---|---| | January | 8.9 h | July | 15.6 h | | February | 10.3 h | August | 14.3 h | | March | 11.9 h | September | 12.6 h | | April | 13.7 h | October | 10.9 h | | May | 15.2 h | November | 9.3 h | | June | 16.0 h | December | 8.4 h | Light is the plant's energy budget. A February seedling under 10 hours of weak, low-angle light has roughly two thirds of the day length a May seedling gets, at a much lower sun angle, and it grows accordingly: a warm February week produces a pale, stretched plant rather than an early one. This is the honest reason that starting too early does not work, and it is why [Starting Seeds](/library#starting-seeds) calls starting too early the beginner's classic mistake. **Rule of thumb, widely used by winter growers and not something anyone has published a measurement for:** below about 10 hours of daylight, most vegetables effectively stop making new growth and simply hold whatever size they had reached. Checked against the Naval Observatory's sunrise and sunset tables for this point, Silverdale drops below ten hours around **October 31** and climbs back above it around **February 10**. That is about 102 days, a little over fourteen weeks, in which a plant in the ground is stored, not growing. That single fact reorganises the whole autumn plan, which is the next section. ## The autumn side, which people plan worse Almost everyone plans spring carefully and autumn by feel, and then wonders why the late sowing never finished. The reason is that spring and autumn are not symmetrical. A spring crop grows into lengthening days and warming soil, so every week is better than the last. An autumn crop grows into shortening days and cooling soil, so every week is worse than the last. A crop sown late does not simply finish late. It slows down, then holds, then sits there through the winter at whatever size it reached. Virginia Cooperative Extension publishes the standard correction for this. Count backwards from your first frost date, and add up: ``` days from seed to transplant (if you are raising your own) + days from transplant to harvest + the average harvest period + about 14 days "fall factor", for slower growth in cooler, shorter days + about 14 days "frost-tender factor", if frost kills this crop = the number of days to count back from your first frost date ``` The fall factor is the piece people leave out. A 50-day crop sown in August is not a 50-day crop; it is closer to a 64-day crop, and if it is frost-tender you want it finished a fortnight before the frost rather than on the day of it. Which crops need the tender factor is not a judgement call. Virginia Extension sorts them: tomato, summer squash, melon, eggplant, cucumber, pepper and okra cannot withstand frost at all. Cabbage, cauliflower, broccoli and Brussels sprouts withstand some cold and several taste better after a frost. Kale, spinach, evergreen bunching onion, lettuce, parsley, parsnip, carrots and salsify may survive all winter in the ground. That last group is the reason the autumn plan is worth doing well. Get them to full size before daylight falls under ten hours, and the garden becomes a refrigerator you harvest from all winter rather than a bed you clear in October. ## A worked Silverdale calendar Everything below is arithmetic on the numbers already given. The working is shown in the last column so you can redo it with your own dates. Days-to-maturity figures are from the extension sources listed at the end; the number on your own packet takes priority over any of them. ### Spring Anchor for frost-tender crops: **May 13** (the 36 F one-in-ten date). If you will cover plants on cold nights, you may use April 24 instead and pull everything forward by 19 days. | Crop | Sow | Plant out | First harvest | The arithmetic | |---|---|---|---|---| | Pea | March 1, direct | n/a | May 5 to May 20 | Soil min 40 F; 65 to 80 days from seed | | Lettuce, leaf | March 15, direct | n/a | April 24 to May 24 | Soil min 35 F; 40 to 70 days from seed | | Broccoli | Feb 25, indoors | April 1 | May 31 to June 10 | 5 weeks indoors; hardy, so the March 29 median is an acceptable plant-out; 60 to 70 days from transplant | | Carrot | April 15, direct | n/a | June 14 to June 24 | Soil min 40 F; 60 to 70 days from seed | | Tomato | April 1, indoors | May 13 | July 17 to Aug 11 | 6 weeks indoors: May 13 minus 42 days; 65 to 90 days from transplant | | Pepper | March 11, indoors | May 13 | July 22 to Aug 6 | 9 weeks indoors: May 13 minus 63 days; 70 to 85 days from transplant | | Bean, snap | When soil hits 60 F | n/a | 50 to 60 days later | Soil-gated, not date-gated. Measure it | | Squash | When soil hits 60 F | n/a | per packet | Same gate as beans | Note what the broccoli row does differently. Broccoli survives frost, so it does not need the 36 F anchor and can go out around the median date, weeks before the tomatoes. Frost tolerance, not the calendar, is what decides which anchor a crop uses. ### Autumn Anchor: **October 26**, the date by which one year in ten has already frosted. The harvest period below is set at 14 days, which is a choice rather than a published figure; lengthen it for a crop you pick from over several weeks. | Crop | Last useful sowing | The arithmetic | |---|---|---| | Lettuce, leaf | about July 30 | 60 days to maturity + 14 harvest + 14 fall factor = 88; Oct 26 minus 88 | | Bean, snap | about July 21 | 55 + 14 + 14 + 14 tender factor = 97; Oct 26 minus 97 | | Spinach, to overwinter | early September | Sized up before daylight drops under ten hours on Oct 31, then held | | Garlic | late October to Nov 10 | Planted in autumn, harvested the following summer | Those computed dates are worth checking against somebody who has already done the counting for this region. WSU Extension's western Washington guidance puts the last bush bean sowing at late July and the last leaf lettuce at mid-August, and gives late October to November 10 for garlic and September for overwintering spinach. Our July 21 for beans lands inside their late-July window, and our July 30 for lettuce is a comfortable fortnight ahead of their last possible date. The formula and the local expertise agree, which is the outcome you want before trusting either. Silverdale's autumn has one more constraint the frost dates do not show. October brings 131 mm of rain and November 225 mm, against 21 mm in July. A crop that needs to dry down, cure or ripen in the field is fighting the rain long before it is fighting the frost. ## Season extension, briefly Row cover, cloches, cold frames, low tunnels and greenhouses all do the same thing: they trap heat and block wind, buying you a few degrees on a cold night and a few weeks at each end of the season. Practically, they let you use the April 24 anchor instead of the May 13 one in spring, and they keep hardy crops in usable condition well past the October 26 date in autumn. What none of them can do is add daylight. A covered bed in December is a warmer bed in December, not a growing one, which is why winter growing is about holding crops that are already full-sized rather than growing new ones. Build the calendar first; add cover to stretch it. Cover is a separate skill and a separate guide. ## How to find YOUR dates The Silverdale numbers above are nobody else's. Here is how to get your own. **1. Get your frost dates from NOAA.** The US Climate Normals are the authority: a suite of products covering thousands of US stations, currently the 1991 to 2020 period, regenerated every ten years. Use the Climate Normals Quick Access tool at `https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/us-climate-normals/`, pick a station near you, and choose the **annual/seasonal** normals. The variables you want are named like this: | Variable | What it gives | |---|---| | `ANN-TMIN-PRBLST-T32FP10/50/90` | Last spring frost, 32 F, at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles | | `ANN-TMIN-PRBFST-T32FP10/50/90` | First autumn frost, 32 F, same three percentiles | | `ANN-TMIN-PRBGSL-T32FP50` | Growing season length | Swap `T32F` for `T36F` to get the honest seedling threshold. **2. Look at how far away your station actually is.** This is the step people skip, and it is why Silverdale's own climate file names its station in full rather than hiding it. The nearest station with a complete temperature and freeze record is at Bremerton, 8.5 km (5.3 miles) due south of Silverdale at 33.5 m elevation. About fifteen stations sit closer, and every one of them is a precipitation-only site with no temperature data at all, so they cannot answer a frost question. A station a few miles away, at a different elevation, on a different side of a hill, is a genuinely different climate. The same file also records that its normals carry NOAA's "Representative" completeness flag rather than "Standard": 20 of the 30 years have a near-complete daily record and four years have substantial gaps that were filled with estimates. That does not make the numbers wrong. It makes them a good estimate rather than an unbroken measurement, and knowing which one you are holding is part of using it well. **3. Get your day length from the Naval Observatory.** Sunrise and sunset for any point and date, free, at `https://aa.usno.navy.mil/`. Ask for a fixed time zone offset with daylight saving disabled, or the spring and autumn clock changes will corrupt your interval arithmetic. **4. Then correct all of it for your own yard.** Published normals describe a point in an instrument shelter, not your garden. How much your ground differs is not small. Silverdale itself sits on a hardiness zone boundary: the ZIP codes for Silverdale, west Bremerton and Poulsbo are 8b, while two ZIPs nearer the Bremerton waterfront are 9a, and shoreline sites on Dyes Inlet run about half a zone warmer than sites a few hundred metres inland or uphill. Half a zone, over a few hundred metres. **Rule of thumb for reading your own ground:** cold air is dense and flows downhill, so hollows and the uphill side of a solid fence collect frost while a slope sheds it. Large water bodies moderate the sites next to them. A south-facing wall radiates stored heat at night. A minimum-maximum thermometer left in the bed you actually plant, read for a couple of seasons, will beat any published table for that bed, and it costs less than one tray of transplants. ## What the hardiness zone does not tell you Silverdale is USDA hardiness zone 8b, and that fact is less useful for this guide than it looks. The USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map shows the average annual extreme minimum winter temperature, drawn as 10 F zones and 5 F half zones, and the 2023 edition uses the 1991 to 2020 period. What it answers is whether a perennial will survive your winter. It is one number about the coldest night of an average year. It is not a statement about when your spring frosts end, when your autumn frosts begin, how long your season is, or how warm your summer gets. Two places can share a zone and have last-frost dates a month apart. Use the zone to choose fruit trees and perennials; use the frost percentiles to choose planting dates. USDA also notes that zone boundaries shifted in 2023 partly because of better data and improved interpolation rather than temperature change alone, which is another reason not to load more meaning onto the zone than it carries. ## How you know it worked - You can say your own 90th-percentile last frost date, not just your average, and you plant tender crops to the former. - You own a soil thermometer and you use it before sowing beans. - You know which of your crops count days to maturity from transplant and which count from sowing, and your sowing dates reflect the difference. - Your autumn sowings include the fall factor, and the hardy ones reach full size before your daylight drops under ten hours. - Your row cover exists and is reachable in the dark before your one-in-ten autumn frost date, not before your average one. When those five are true you are no longer planting on faith or on somebody else's regional chart. You are planting on arithmetic done with your own numbers, and that arithmetic transfers unchanged to any crop you ever grow and any place you ever move to. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot, so every fact taken from them is restated here in our own words. ### United States government (public domain) - National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, National Centers for Environmental Information. 1991-2020 U.S. Climate Normals, product overview and Quick Access tool (what the normals are, the 1991-2020 period, the ten-year regeneration cycle, and how to look up a station). https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/us-climate-normals and https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/us-climate-normals/ - NOAA NCEI. 1991-2020 Annual/Seasonal Climate Normals, station USC00450872 (Bremerton, WA): freeze and frost probability dates at the 32 F and 36 F thresholds and growing season length. Every frost date and season length in this guide comes from here, by way of `data/locales/silverdale_wa/climate.json`. https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-annualseasonal/1991-2020/access/USC00450872.csv - NOAA NCEI. 1991-2020 Monthly Climate Normals, station USC00450872: the monthly temperature and precipitation figures quoted for Silverdale. https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-monthly/1991-2020/access/USC00450872.csv - NOAA NCEI. Normals variable documentation, which defines PRBLST, PRBFST and PRBGSL and fixes the percentile convention that the whole first half of this guide depends on. https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-annualseasonal/1991-2020/doc/Readme_By-Variable_By-Station_Normals_Files.txt - United States Naval Observatory, Astronomical Applications Department. Sunrise and sunset data for 47.6448 N, 122.6949 W: the monthly daylight column, and the October 31 and February 10 ten-hour crossings computed for this guide. https://aa.usno.navy.mil/ - USDA Agricultural Research Service. Plant Hardiness Zone Map (what the zones measure, the 1991-2020 period behind the 2023 edition, and the note on shifted boundaries). https://planthardiness.ars.usda.gov/ and https://planthardiness.ars.usda.gov/pages/map-creation ### University extension services (copyrighted; cited, not copied) - University of Maryland Extension, When to Plant Vegetables (the days-to-maturity convention, and which crops count from transplanting rather than from direct seeding; the 60 F soil minimum for beans, cucumbers and melons). https://extension.umd.edu/resource/when-plant-vegetables - University of Maryland Extension, Growing Tomatoes in a Home Garden (65 to 90 days from transplant). https://extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-tomatoes-home-garden - University of Maryland Extension, Growing Peppers in a Home Garden (70 to 85 days from transplanting; 8 to 10 weeks indoors before the average frost-free date). https://extension.umd.edu/resource/growing-peppers-home-garden - Utah State University Extension, Tomatoes in the Garden (6 to 8 weeks to grow transplants; transplant when soil is above 60 F or frost danger has passed; transplants mature about four weeks ahead of direct-seeded plants). https://extension.usu.edu/yardandgarden/research/tomatoes-in-the-garden - Utah State University Extension, Peppers in the Garden (8 to 10 weeks to grow transplants; 60 F soil at transplanting). https://extension.usu.edu/yardandgarden/research/peppers-in-the-garden - Clemson University Home and Garden Information Center, Planning a Garden (days to harvest for lettuce, radish, spinach, snap bean, carrot, beet, broccoli, kale and pea, and whether each counts from seed or from transplant). https://hgic.clemson.edu/factsheet/planning-a-garden/ - Alabama Cooperative Extension System, Soil Temperature Conditions for Vegetable Seed Germination (the minimum and optimum soil temperature table). The same table is published by Oregon State University Extension as Soil Temperature Conditions for Vegetable Seed Germination. https://www.aces.edu/blog/topics/lawn-garden/soil-temperature-conditions-for-vegetable-seed-germination/ and https://extension.oregonstate.edu/gardening/soil-compost/soil-temperature-conditions-vegetable-seed-germination - Virginia Cooperative Extension, Fall Vegetable Gardening, publication 426-334 (the count-back formula, the fall factor and frost-tender factor of about two weeks each, and the frost-tolerance groupings). https://ext.vt.edu/content/pubs_ext_vt_edu/en/426/426-334/426-334.html - Washington State University Extension, Snohomish County, Fall and Winter Vegetable Gardens for Western Washington (the regional last sowing dates used as a cross-check: bush beans by late July, leaf lettuce until mid-August, garlic late October to November 10, spinach in September to winter over). https://extension.wsu.edu/snohomish/fall-and-winter-vegetable-gardens-for-western-washington/ ### Inside this project - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/climate.json`, which holds every Silverdale figure quoted here along with its full provenance, including which station was used, how far away it is, and how complete its record is. - [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa), the generated gazetteer, for the soils, hydrology and hazards that this guide only touches. - [Starting Seeds](/library#starting-seeds) for the indoor weeks per crop and for hardening off, and [Your First Tomato](/library#your-first-tomato) for what happens after the transplant goes in. ### Labelled in the text as rules of thumb, not sourced - The ten-hour daylight threshold as the point where growth effectively stops. The daylight figures themselves are from the Naval Observatory; the threshold is a winter-growing convention that nobody has published a measurement for. - The 14-day harvest period used in the autumn arithmetic. Virginia Extension's formula asks for the average harvest period without giving a number; 14 days is a placeholder you should replace per crop. - Soil lagging air temperature, and cold air pooling in hollows. Both are standard and neither is quoted here from a specific measurement.
