docs.text: # Firewood Three decisions make up this whole subject: **how much wood you need, what it is, and when you cut it.** Everything else is consequence. Get the quantity wrong and you run out in February. Get the moisture wrong and you burn twice the wood for half the heat and line your chimney with tar. Get the species wrong and you have merely wasted effort, which is the mildest failure here. So, the short answer, and the rest of this guide is why. **How much.** The Forest Products Laboratory puts the energy used to heat an average-sized home at between 50 and 150 million Btu over a heating season, and rates seasoned firewood at about 15.3 million Btu of *usable* heat per cord once stove losses are taken off. Divide one by the other: **roughly 3 to 10 cords a year**, with their own worked example of a 100-million-Btu season coming out at 6.5 cords. Six cords stacked four feet high and sixteen inches deep is about 144 feet of wall. Go and look at 144 feet of anything before you decide you have enough wood. **Of what.** Locally, Douglas-fir, with bigleaf maple its equal and red alder its easy-splitting understudy. Western redcedar is the one species here you should mostly *not* burn for heat, for reasons in the species section. **Cut when.** As far ahead as you can stand. A year ahead is the working answer; the real answer is whenever a moisture meter says the wood is under 20 percent, and nothing else. Where a number appears below it comes from a publication that measured it, listed in the Sources at the bottom. Where something is a working rule rather than a measured value, it says so. Two things this guide deliberately does not do. It **does not teach tree felling**, which is the part of firewood that kills people, and it says so again with more force further down. And it does not repeat the companion guides: species properties, moisture content and decay are in [Working with Wood](/library#working-with-wood); axe and saw filing are in [Sharpening](/library#sharpening); the heat you are trying to keep in the building is in [Insulation and Heat Loss](/library#insulation-and-heat-loss); and the air the fire needs, plus the full treatment of carbon monoxide, is in [Ventilation, Damp and Mould](/library#ventilation-damp-and-mould). That last pairing matters more than it sounds and has its own section here. ## The unit problem, which is where people get cheated Start here, because this is the one part of the subject with a legal answer, and it is the part most buyers do not know. **A cord is a defined volume.** NIST Handbook 130, the model regulation that state weights-and-measures agencies adopt, defines it at section 2.4.1.2 as the amount of wood contained in a space of 128 cubic feet when the wood is ranked, with individual pieces touching and parallel to each other and stacked in a compact manner. Four feet by four feet by eight feet. The words "ranked" and "compact" are doing work: a heaped pile of the same wood occupies more space and is not a cord. **Firewood may only be sold by that measure.** Section 2.4.3 requires fireplace and stove wood to be advertised, offered for sale and sold only by the cord or the cubic metre. The exceptions are narrow: packaged natural wood under 0.45 cubic metres, which is an eighth of a cord or 16 cubic feet, is declared in litres; compressed or processed logs and bricks over 6 inches in any dimension go by weight plus count; pellets and chips under 6 inches go by weight. **The informal units are prohibited outright.** Section 2.4.4 is titled Prohibition of Terms and states that the listed terms shall not be used when advertising, offering for sale, or selling wood for use as fuel. The Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection, restating the same model regulation as its state rule, gives the list as face cord, rack, pile, truckload, or terms of similar import. Here is why that ban exists, in one table. The only sourced row is the first; the rest is arithmetic on the cord definition, using piece lengths and a truck bed I chose for illustration. | What you are offered | The stack it describes | Cubic feet | Fraction of a cord | |---|---|---|---| | Cord | 4 ft x 4 ft x 8 ft, ranked | 128 | 1 | | "Face cord" or "rick" of 12 inch pieces | 4 x 8 ft face, 1 ft deep | 32 | one quarter | | "Face cord" or "rick" of 16 inch pieces | 4 x 8 ft face, 16 in deep | 42.7 | one third | | "Face cord" or "rick" of 24 inch pieces | 4 x 8 ft face, 2 ft deep | 64 | one half | | Level pickup load, 8 ft bed, 4 ft usable width, 1.5 ft sides | 8 x 4 x 1.5 ft | 48 | about three eighths | A face cord is not a unit. It is a face of unknown depth, and the same words can mean a quarter of a cord or half of one depending on a number nobody said out loud. **A "truckload" is worth even less as a promise,** because it describes a vehicle rather than a volume: the level pickup load above is about three eighths of a cord, and a heaped one is a guess. **What you are owed on delivery.** Section 2.4.5 requires a delivery ticket or sales invoice whenever any non-packaged firewood is sold, and it must carry the vendor's name and address, the purchaser's name and address, the date delivered, the quantity delivered and the quantity the price is based on if those differ, the price, and the identity of the wood in the most descriptive terms commercially practicable, including any quality claim made in the sale. **What you are owed on species.** Section 2.4.2 allows a seller to declare a species group, giving the regulation's own example of 50 percent hickory and 50 percent miscellaneous softwood, and requires that declaration to be accurate within 10 percent. So "mixed hardwood" that arrives as cottonwood is not a matter of opinion. The practical move: buy by the cord, get it stacked or stack it yourself before the truck leaves, and measure the stack. Four by four by eight. If the seller will not sell by the cord, they are not offering you a unit. ## Moisture content decides everything else If you take one number from this guide, take this one: **under 20 percent.** EPA's Burn Wise programme states it plainly, that wood burns best at a moisture content of less than 20 percent, and tells you not to burn wet or green wood at all. Here is what that is worth, from the Forest Products Laboratory's Fuel Value Calculator. Gross heating value is the energy in the fuel; the efficiency column is what a typical appliance gets out of it; the last column is what you actually receive. | Condition | Moisture content | Gross, million Btu per ton | Efficiency | Usable, million Btu per ton | |---|---|---|---|---| | Green | 50% | 8.60 | 67% | 5.74 | | Semidried | 30% | 12.04 | 74% | 8.95 | | Air-dried | 20% | 13.76 | 77% | 10.56 | | Ovendry | 0% | 17.20 | 80% | 13.80 | Read the first and third rows together. **A ton of air-dried wood delivers 84 percent more usable heat than a ton of green wood.** Same tree, same species, same truck. And you paid to haul the difference, because, as the same publication says, water commonly makes up half the weight of a living tree. Two separate mechanisms are stacked in that table, and it is worth pulling them apart because they are fixed by the same action for different reasons. The larger one is simply **mass**. Green wood at 50 percent moisture on a wet basis is half water by weight, so a ton of it contains half a ton of fuel, and the gross column duly halves from 17.20 to 8.60. You are paying to cut, split, stack, carry and haul water. The smaller one is the **efficiency** column, which drops from 80 percent ovendry to 67 percent green, a further penalty of about a sixth. That is the latent heat of vaporisation: the fire must boil the water out of the wood before the wood will burn. FPL is explicit that in the operation of heating boilers the flue gas temperature is generally kept high enough to prevent the water vapour condensing, and that the latent heat of vaporisation is therefore **not available for making steam, hot water or useful heat.** It goes up the chimney. You never get it back. ### The two different 20 percents This trips people up and it is worth thirty seconds. Moisture content can be expressed on a **dry basis**, as water weight divided by the wood's ovendry weight, which is the convention in the Wood Handbook and in the moisture meter you will buy; it is why green wood can read over 100 percent. Or it can be expressed on a **wet basis**, as water divided by total weight, which the Fuel Value Calculator above uses and says so. Converting between them is one line of arithmetic. Twenty percent on a dry basis is 16.7 percent wet; twenty percent wet is 25 percent dry. So the FPL "20 percent" row is slightly wetter wood than the EPA "under 20 percent" target that your meter is reading. The gap is small and both point the same way, but knowing which convention a number uses is the difference between reading a table and guessing at it. ### What wet wood does to the chimney Smoke is unburned fuel. A fire that is boiling water is a fire that is not hot enough to burn its own smoke, so the unburned fraction goes up the flue, meets surfaces cooler than itself, and plates out. The Consumer Product Safety Commission describes the result exactly: creosote, a tarry substance condensed inside the chimney and chimney connectors. That is the whole causal chain, and it is why moisture is a safety topic rather than an economy topic. Wet wood makes smoke; smoke makes creosote; creosote is what chimney fires burn. The creosote section below has the numbers. ## Seasoning: how long, stacked how, covered how **How long is the wrong question and everybody asks it anyway.** The honest answer is that "a year" is a rule of thumb that happens to work in most places. EPA says to season wood for at least six months. Washington's Department of Ecology, which is writing for this climate specifically, says to use wood that has been split, covered and stacked for at least one year. USDA APHIS, surveying the trade for a different purpose entirely, reports that seasoned wood has generally been air dried for six months to a year, though wood cut in winter and dried under good conditions may be considered seasoned after three months. Three federal and state bodies, three different answers, all correct, because drying time depends on species, piece size, climate and how the stack is built. **The real answer is a moisture meter**, which EPA recommends by name and which costs less than a wheelbarrow. Split a piece, press the probes into the freshly exposed face, and read it. The outside of a stacked round tells you nothing; the inside is what burns. **Split it first, and split it soon.** Bark is the tree's own weather seal and it works after death. Splitting opens the wet interior to the air and multiplies the exposed surface. Green wood also splits more willingly than seasoned wood, so the work is easier now than later. **Stack it off the ground, and stack it single-row.** EPA's instruction is to store wood outdoors, off the ground, with only the top covered, because covering the sides traps moisture in. That last clause is the one people get backwards: a tarp over the whole pile is a humidity tent. You want a roof, not a bag. Off the ground matters for the same reason it matters in [Working with Wood](/library#working-with-wood): serious decay needs liquid water and wood above about 30 percent moisture content, and ground contact is the most reliable way to supply both. Rot is fungi eating your fuel before you do. **Why the ends matter.** Wood is not equally permeable in all directions. The Wood Handbook makes the point about water going in, that absorption is most rapid in the longitudinal direction, meaning through the end grain, and the same anisotropy governs water coming out. The ends are the motorway; the sides are a footpath. Which gives three practical rules that follow directly: cut to length before stacking rather than after, leave the cut ends exposed to moving air rather than butted against each other or against a wall, and expect the checks that open in the end grain as it dries. Those checks are the wood telling you the ends are working. **What this climate does to the ceiling.** Wood outdoors does not dry to whatever you want; it equilibrates with the air. [Working with Wood](/library#working-with-wood), quoting the Wood Handbook, gives the outdoor equilibrium figures for Seattle as 12.0 percent in July rising to 16.9 percent in December. So in western Washington, **under 20 percent is achievable and 8 percent is not**, and a stack left uncovered through a Silverdale winter climbs back toward 17 percent no matter how well it dried in August. The locale's own rainfall record makes the same point another way: December averages 252 mm of precipitation against 21 mm in July. Cover the top, and bring a week's wood inside ahead of burning it. ## Heat by species, which is a density story Here is the fact that dissolves most firewood folklore: **a pound of wood is a pound of wood.** The Fuel Value Calculator gives ovendry wood a single gross heating value of 17.2 million Btu per ton, about 8,600 Btu per pound, with no species column at all. The Wood Handbook makes the parallel point about moisture behaviour, that for most practical purposes its equilibrium moisture content values may be applied to wood of any species. The USDA APHIS firewood assessment says it from the trade side: although some species are preferred based on characteristics like heat production and splitting, all species of trees can be and are used as firewood. So the differences between species in a stove are not differences of quality. **They are differences of density**, because a cord is a fixed volume and denser wood puts more pounds of fuel into it. The specific gravities below are from the Wood Handbook's Table 5-3b, at 12 percent moisture content, defined there as ovendry weight over volume at that moisture content. The last two columns are my arithmetic on those numbers: ovendry pounds per cubic foot is specific gravity times 62.4, a cord is taken as holding about 80 cubic feet of solid wood, which is a **rule of thumb** and not a measured value, and the heat is 8,600 Btu per pound. The cross-check is reassuring: Douglas-fir comes out at 20.6 million Btu per cord against the Fuel Value Calculator's 20 million for "seasoned firewood", so the rule of thumb is in the right place. | Species | Specific gravity at 12% | Estimated million Btu per cord | Relative to Douglas-fir | |---|---|---|---| | Douglas-fir (Coast) | 0.48 | 20.6 | 1.00 | | Bigleaf maple | 0.48 | 20.6 | 1.00 | | Western hemlock | 0.45 | 19.3 | 0.94 | | Red alder | 0.41 | 17.6 | 0.85 | | Lodgepole pine | 0.41 | 17.6 | 0.85 | | Sitka spruce | 0.40 | 17.2 | 0.83 | | Grand fir | 0.37 | 15.9 | 0.77 | | Black cottonwood | 0.35 | 15.0 | 0.73 | | Western redcedar | 0.32 | 13.7 | 0.67 | One naming note on that table: the shore pine that grows on this coast is *Pinus contorta*, the same species as the handbook's lodgepole pine, in a different variety. The row is close enough to use and not the same tree. Notice the spread. From the best to the worst on that list is a factor of about 1.5, not a factor of ten. A cord of cedar is not worthless; it is two thirds of a cord of Douglas-fir, and it will heat your house if that is what you have. The folklore that treats softwood as unburnable is wrong, and it is wrong in a way the table makes obvious. How to read that table for what is actually in these woods: **Split for heat: Douglas-fir and bigleaf maple.** Tied at the top and both abundant here. Douglas-fir is the default firewood of this region for the straightforward reason that it is the region's dominant timber tree and there is always some coming down. **Split for heat, but burn it sooner: western hemlock.** Ninety four percent of Douglas-fir's heat, which is fine. The catch is not in this table but in the companion guide's: hemlock heartwood is rated slightly or nonresistant to decay, so a hemlock stack that gets rained on is composting. Cover it and burn it within the year. **Split for heat, and enjoy the work: red alder.** Eighty five percent, which is a real but modest penalty, in exchange for a wood that splits cleanly, seasons fast and grows back everywhere a disturbance happens. The locale species record notes that red alder coals are the standard wood for smoking salmon in this region, which is a second use for the same woodpile. **Do not split for heat: western redcedar.** It is last on the table at two thirds, but that is not the argument. The argument is that cedar is the only species in this region whose heartwood the Wood Handbook rates decay-resistant, and it has the least shrinkage of the lot, which is why it is the wood for siding, shakes, fence boards, raised beds and anything that has to sit outside and stay flat. **Burning structural cedar is burning the most valuable board in the woods to make the least heat in the table.** What cedar is genuinely excellent at is kindling: it splits into thin straight sticks along the grain and lights from a match. Two working cautions that are trade knowledge rather than sourced findings: cedar snaps and throws sparks as it burns, so keep the screen closed, and cedar dust is a respiratory hazard, which [Working with Wood](/library#working-with-wood) covers under the same NIOSH entry as wood dust generally. **Take it if it is down, do not go looking: black cottonwood, grand fir.** Three quarters of Douglas-fir, wet and stringy when green, perfectly serviceable once dry. A lot of handling per unit of heat. **Oregon white oak is the exception to all of the above.** The locale species record describes it as a hard, heavy wood used for fuel and tool handles, which by the density logic would make it the best firewood here. It is not in the Wood Handbook's table, so this guide gives it no number. The same record describes it as local and patchy on the Kitsap Peninsula rather than widespread, confined to dry prairie edges and open south facing slopes, and it supports deer, squirrels and birds. Take it if a tree is already down. Do not take one down for fuel. ## What a cord is worth against other fuels Worth knowing before you commit a winter to it, because the answer is lopsided in one direction and the catch is not in the price. The Forest Products Laboratory's Fuel Value Calculator works the comparison for a 100 million Btu heating season, at its own example prices. **Those prices are illustrative and old, and every one of them has moved**, so read the ordering rather than the dollars. | Fuel | Appliance efficiency | Example price | Cost for the season | |---|---|---|---| | Seasoned firewood | 77% | $115 per cord | $747 | | Natural gas | 80% | $7 per 1,000 cubic feet | $854 | | Premium wood pellets | 83% | $120 per ton | $882 | | Fuel oil #2 | 83% | $1.40 per gallon | $1,220 | | Propane | 79% | $1.25 per gallon | $1,730 | | Electricity | 98% | $0.08 per kWh | $2,390 | FPL's own conclusion is that seasoned firewood is the least expensive fuel, with natural gas and wood pellets a close second and third. And its own caveat is the honest one: to decide whether firewood is the fuel of choice you have to compare the heating systems too, and work out how much time and effort you are willing to spend processing and handling the fuel, because fossil fuel heating systems typically cost less up front, sometimes significantly so, than firewood and wood pellet furnaces. That is the shape of the trade. **Wood is cheap per Btu and expensive per hour.** Nothing on that list except pellets asks you to cut, split, stack, turn, carry and sweep. Six cords is not a purchase; it is a season of weekends, and an oil tank is not. For scale, the Energy Information Administration's 2012 survey found about 2.5 million United States households, 2.1 percent, using wood as their main heating fuel, up from 1.7 percent in 2005, with a further 9 million households, 7.7 percent, burning it as a secondary fuel. Together that is roughly 500 trillion Btu a year, about the same as residential propane and slightly less than fuel oil. Heating stoves are the commonest equipment for households whose main heat is wood; fireplaces are the commonest for secondary heat. ## Creosote and chimney fires Fire is the ordinary failure of this whole subject, and the chimney is where it happens. The US Fire Administration's topical report on heating fires in residential buildings puts the 2017 to 2019 average at **34,200 heating fires a year in residential buildings, causing 165 deaths, 600 injuries and $367 million in property loss**. Its separate figures for 2021 are 32,200 fires, 190 deaths, 625 injuries and $442 million. **Heating is the second leading cause of all residential building fires, following cooking**, and incidence peaks in January at 20 percent of the year's total. Now the number that matters for this section. In that same data, **confined fires, meaning those confined to chimneys, flues or fuel burners, accounted for 77 percent of residential building heating fires**, and the report's own breakdown puts chimney or flue fires at 49.4 percent of the total against 27.2 percent for confined fuel burner or boiler malfunctions. Just under half of every home heating fire in the United States is a fire inside the chimney. That is the whole case for the maintenance below, and it is unusual to get a risk this concentrated and this cheap to fix. The other headline from the same report belongs here too: in the *nonconfined* fires, the ones that got out into the building, **the heat source was too close to combustibles 27 percent of the time.** That is what the three foot clearance rule exists to prevent, and it is worth reading as the second half of this section: keep the fire inside the chimney, and keep the building away from the fire. **What creosote is and how it forms.** CPSC calls it a tarry substance condensed inside chimneys and chimney connectors, and "condensed" is the operative word. Smoke is unburned fuel in vapour and particle form. When it touches flue surfaces below the temperature at which it stays airborne, it deposits. So anything that makes more smoke, or a cooler flue, makes more creosote. **What actually reduces it**, in order of how much difference it makes: 1. **Burn dry wood.** This is most of it. See the section above: wet wood is smoke by definition, because the fire is spending its heat boiling water instead of burning the volatiles. 2. **Burn hot, not slow.** The classic mistake is damping a stove right down overnight for a long burn. A starved fire is an incompletely burning fire, and incompletely burned fuel is what ends up on the flue wall. It is also the same condition that produces carbon monoxide, which is the next section. 3. **Burn wood, and only wood.** USFA is direct: do not burn paper in your fireplace or wood stove. Paper, cardboard and rubbish burn fast, throw embers up the flue, and can ignite deposits already there. Treated, painted or salvaged construction lumber adds a chemistry problem to a fire problem. 4. **Have the chimney swept and inspected every year.** This one is not a preference. USFA says to have heating equipment and chimneys cleaned and inspected each year by a professional. CPSC says to have flues and chimneys inspected before each heating season for leakage and blockage by creosote or debris. CDC says to have the chimney checked or cleaned every year, and CDC is saying it for a different reason, which is the next section. Three federal agencies, three different remits, the same annual interval. **And put the fire out before you sleep.** USFA's wording is exactly that: put the fire out before you go to sleep or leave your home. CPSC adds the matching rule about the other end of the burn, never to close the damper or go to bed while the ashes are still warm, because an open damper helps prevent the build-up of poisonous gases indoors. **Ashes.** USFA: put ashes in a metal container with a lid, and place the container outside at least 10 feet from your home. Not a cardboard box, not a plastic bin, not the wheeled rubbish cart, and not on a wooden deck. Ash holds live embers for days. ## Carbon monoxide, which is the part that kills Everything above burns buildings. This burns people, quietly, in their sleep. Carbon monoxide is produced whenever carbon-based fuel burns. It is colourless, odourless and tasteless, which is why USFA calls it the invisible killer. CDC lists the early symptoms as headache, dizziness, weakness, upset stomach, vomiting, chest pain and confusion, which is also a description of winter flu, and that overlap is exactly the danger. The numbers, from three agencies counting different things: - **CDC**, on unintentional poisoning not linked to fires: more than 400 Americans die each year, more than 100,000 visit an emergency department, and more than 14,000 are hospitalised. - **USFA**: more than 150 people in the United States die every year from accidental non-fire-related carbon monoxide. - **CPSC**, counting only heating systems, ranges and ovens, and water heaters: an average of about 85 deaths a year. ### The three ways a wood fire does it **A blocked or damaged flue.** The exhaust has nowhere to go, so it comes back into the room. A bird's nest, a collapsed liner, a chimney that was never swept, or, as USFA specifically warns, a vent buried in snow or debris. This is the failure mode the annual inspection above is really for: the sweep is not only removing fuel for a chimney fire, they are confirming the flue is open. **A starved fire.** A fire damped down for a long slow burn is a fire running short of oxygen, and incomplete combustion is what makes carbon monoxide rather than carbon dioxide. The overnight damp-down that lays creosote in your chimney is producing carbon monoxide at the same time, by the same mechanism. Those are not two problems. They are one problem with two symptoms. **An unvented fire indoors.** CDC's rule is absolute: do not cook or burn anything on a stove or fireplace that is not vented. A camp stove, a charcoal grill, a patio heater or an unflued propane heater brought inside during a power cut puts every combustion product into the room you are breathing. This is the classic winter-storm death and it happens every year. ### Where this meets the insulation guide This is the pair those two documents form, and it is worth stating directly. [Insulation and Heat Loss](/library#insulation-and-heat-loss) tells you to air seal before you insulate, because air leakage is roughly a third of a building's heat loss and sealing it is the cheapest comfort you will ever buy. That advice is correct and you should follow it. But a wood stove with a conventional flue is a **natural draft appliance**: it relies on hot gas rising to pull exhaust up the chimney, and it takes the air it needs from the room. Tighten the building around it, or add a powerful range hood or an exhaust-only ventilation fan, and you can depressurise the house enough that the flue reverses and the exhaust comes **down** the chimney instead. A leaky old house shrugs that off. A well-sealed one does not. [Ventilation, Damp and Mould](/library#ventilation-damp-and-mould) has the full treatment, including the fixes in order of how well they work and the alarm requirements. The short version: if you air seal a house that has a wood stove in it, get the combustion appliances checked afterwards, and consider a dedicated outside air supply for the stove. ### Alarms Not optional, and not the same device as a smoke alarm. USFA: install carbon monoxide alarms in a central location outside each separate sleeping area and on every level of your home. CDC: check the batteries when the clocks change each spring and autumn, and **replace the alarm itself following the manufacturer's instructions or every 5 years**. A carbon monoxide sensor wears out on a schedule whether it has ever detected anything or not. If it sounds, get everyone outside into fresh air first, then call emergency services from outside. Do not go back in to investigate. ## Wood smoke is a health problem, not a smell It is easy to treat smoke as a nuisance, a thing neighbours complain about. The evidence says otherwise, and the affected people are not abstract. EPA is direct that the biggest health threat from smoke is fine particles, also called fine particulate matter or PM2.5. Those particles are small enough to reach the eyes and the deep respiratory system, and EPA attributes to them burning eyes, runny nose, and illnesses such as bronchitis; the ability to make asthma symptoms worse and trigger asthma attacks; and the ability to trigger heart attacks, stroke, irregular heart rhythms and heart failure, especially in people already at risk. Wood smoke also carries benzene, formaldehyde, acrolein and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons. EPA's list of who is at greater risk is worth reading slowly, because it is probably a description of somebody on your street: children, teenagers and older adults; people with lung disease including asthma and COPD; people with heart disease; outdoor workers; people of low socioeconomic status including people who are homeless; people with obesity or diabetes; and pregnant women. This is not an argument against heating with wood. It is the argument for doing it properly, and the single biggest lever is the same one as everywhere else in this guide: **dry wood, burned hot, in a certified appliance, makes very little smoke.** EPA says exactly that, that dry seasoned wood creates very little smoke and that the more efficiently you burn, the less smoke is created. ### Burn bans Where enough households burn wood in a valley that holds air still, the smoke becomes a regional air quality problem and the response is a burn ban. In western Washington, the Puget Sound Clean Air Agency holds the authority to issue air quality burn bans for King, Kitsap, Pierce and Snohomish counties, and describes wood smoke as a main contributor to harmful fine particle pollution. Restating its two stages in our own words, because a state or regional agency's text is not public domain: - **Stage 1** stops all outdoor burning and all burning in wood-burning fireplaces, uncertified wood stoves and uncertified fireplace inserts. A certified stove may still be used, but it may not produce visible smoke. - **Stage 2** stops burning in *any* wood-burning fireplace, wood stove or fireplace insert, certified or not, and in pellet stoves as well. Both stages have an exemption for a household whose wood heat is its only adequate source of heat, and the Washington Department of Ecology describes the same structure statewide. Two practical consequences: **the exemption has to be applied for and approved before a ban is called**, not claimed during one, and if wood is genuinely your only heat, that application is a piece of paperwork worth doing in September rather than January. Ecology also notes that selling an uncertified wood stove is illegal in Washington, although removing one is not required when a house changes hands. Find out how your local agency announces bans and sign up for the alert before you need it. ## Getting the wood: the part that hurts people ### Felling **This guide does not teach tree felling and you should not learn it from a document.** That is a hard boundary, the same one [Building a Fire Staff](/library#fire-staff-materials) draws around fire spinning. Dropping a tree is a skill with a fatal failure mode, it is learned in person from someone competent, and no amount of reading substitutes. What follows is only enough to tell you what competence looks like, so you can recognise its absence. Federal workplace regulation, OSHA 29 CFR 1910.266, is the closest thing to a public-domain statement of the standard of care, and four of its provisions tell you most of what you need to know about why this is dangerous. **The dead standing tree is the most dangerous one to take.** The regulation defines a **danger tree** as a standing tree that presents a hazard due to conditions such as deterioration or physical damage to the root system, trunk, stem or limbs, and the direction and lean of the tree. It requires the employer to fell, remove or avoid each one; if it is neither felled nor removed it must be marked, and **no work may be conducted within two tree lengths of it.** Before felling, a danger tree must be carefully checked for loose bark, broken branches and limbs, and other damage. Read that against the instinct that says a dead tree is the polite one to cut because it is already dead. The dead tree is the one with rotten hinge wood that will not steer, loose bark that will not hold a wedge, and broken limbs waiting overhead. The regulation's answer to a danger tree is to keep two tree lengths away from it. **You must have a planned escape route before you start.** The regulation requires the feller to plan and clear a retreat path before felling begins, extending diagonally away from the expected felling line. Not straight back, which is where the butt goes; diagonally. **The cuts are specified because guessing at them kills.** An undercut in each tree, sized so the tree will not split and will fall in the intended direction, and a backcut leaving sufficient hinge wood to hold the tree to the stump during most of its fall so the hinge can guide it. The hinge is the steering. A tree cut through is a tree nobody is steering. **Nobody works alone.** The regulation requires each employee to work within visual or audible contact with another employee, and requires that no one approach closer than two tree lengths to a tree being felled until the feller says it is safe. A first-aid kit is required at each site where trees are being cut. If you are going to fell trees, get trained. Until then, cut wood that is already on the ground, and stay two tree lengths away from anything standing that looks wrong. ### The chainsaw The same regulation is unusually specific about chainsaws, and its list is a good self-audit whether or not you are anyone's employee. - **Leg protection of cut-resistant material, such as ballistic nylon, covering the full length of the thigh to the top of the boot on each leg.** This is the one piece of equipment people skip, and it is protecting the limb the saw is closest to. - **Foot protection** that covers and supports the ankle, and for chainsaw operators, built of cut-resistant material. - **Eye and head protection** where there is potential for injury from falling or flying objects, which with a chainsaw is always. - **Start it on the ground or otherwise firmly supported, with the chain brake engaged. Drop starting is prohibited.** Start at least 10 feet from where you fuelled it. - **Both hands, thumbs and fingers encircling the handles**, throughout operation. - **Shut it down or engage the chain brake whenever you carry it further than 50 feet.** - **Shut it off or release the throttle before you start your retreat.** On kickback, which is the mechanism behind the worst of these injuries: CPSC describes it as the sudden swift movement of the saw blade up and back toward the user, and estimated 105,000 chainsaw injuries requiring medical attention in 1979, of which about 24,000 were kickback injuries. That data is decades old and saws have changed a great deal since, chain brakes and low-kickback chain among the changes; CPSC found at the time that a redesigned chain cut kickback energy by as much as 74 percent. The number is dated. The mechanism is not. ### Splitting and bucking Less dramatic than a chainsaw and a great deal more routine, which is exactly why people relax around it. Three points, all of them consequences of things taught elsewhere: **A dull axe is the dangerous axe.** That is the whole thesis of [Sharpening](/library#sharpening), which also gives the axe bevel, the filing direction, and the reason never to put an axe on a high-speed dry bench grinder. This guide will not re-teach it. **Split against something that will not throw the piece back.** A chopping block that puts the workpiece at a height where a missed swing goes into the block or the ground, not into your shin. **Wood splits along the grain, and knots are where it refuses to.** [Working with Wood](/library#working-with-wood) explains why: wood is enormously strong along the fibres and weak across them, and a knot is a region where the fibres are distorted around a branch. A round that will not split is usually a round with a knot in the line you are hitting. Move the line, or set that round aside for a hydraulic splitter or a longer burn. ## Moving firewood, and why it is a rule rather than a slogan "Buy it where you burn it" sounds like a bumper sticker. It is a quarantine rule, and the reasoning behind it is specific. Insects and fungi live in wood. Felling a tree does not kill them. USDA APHIS's risk assessment on the movement of firewood puts it plainly: pests that attack live trees often survive tree felling, rough processing and shipping, and pests may also attack the wood afterwards, in the landing, during transport, or lying in a firewood yard. Seasoning does not solve it either; the same assessment notes that wood infested with emerald ash borer may hold both new and fully developed larvae, and that it can take two successive emergence periods, meaning two summers, for all the adults to emerge. Pine wood nematodes can survive 20 months in chipped wood. The reason this matters is that firewood moves at highway speed and insects do not. APHIS cites an estimate that firewood spread is frequently 150 to 200 miles, and surveys finding that between 8 and 57 percent of campers bring firewood from home, often travelling 100 to 200 miles and frequently crossing state lines. Research in the western states estimated **330,000 campers moving firewood into national parks every year.** An insect that disperses at its own flying speed gets two hundred miles in an afternoon instead, and arrives somewhere nothing has evolved to resist it. That is why the regulation exists. The same assessment reports that 28 states in the lower 48 have quarantine regulations covering the movement of raw logs, with newer ones naming firewood explicitly, and lists the organisms that prompted federal and state quarantines: emerald ash borer, Asian longhorned beetle, spongy moth (the species APHIS calls gypsy moth in that 2011 document), pine shoot beetle, sudden oak death, sirex wood wasp, hemlock woolly adelgid and European larch canker. New York was the first state to prohibit moving untreated firewood more than 50 miles. **Heat treatment is the exception that proves the rule.** Firewood imported into the United States must generally undergo heat treatment at 71.1 degrees C for 75 minutes. For domestic firewood, the assessment cites thermotolerance work on emerald ash borer concluding that an internal wood temperature of 60 degrees C for 60 minutes should be considered the minimum for safe treatment. Certified heat-treated bundles carry a seal and may travel. So, in practice: **source your firewood locally, burn it where you got it, and do not carry a load of it to a campsite or across a state line.** If you are going camping, buy it at the campground or from a certified treated source. Check whether your county or state is inside a quarantine before you move any wood at all; APHIS and your state agriculture department both publish the current areas. ## Storing it **Away from the house.** USFA's wildfire guidance is to keep the first 5 feet around a home clear of anything flammable, and it names woodpiles first on the list. By the arithmetic in the species table above, a cord of seasoned Douglas-fir weighs close to a ton and a half, and every ounce of it is dry fuel with an enormous surface area. Stacked against the house it sits exactly where you least want it in a wildfire, and directly under the eaves in an ember shower. Put the main stack well away, and keep only a few days of wood close in. **Off the ground.** Pallets, rails, gravel, anything. Ground contact wicks water into the bottom course and holds it there, which puts that wood back above the moisture content where decay fungi work. You are trying to keep the fuel under 20 percent; the ground is trying to put it over 30. **Not stacked against a wall, and this is two mistakes at once.** The moisture half is straightforward: a wall blocks air on one side, so that face of the stack does not dry, and the stack traps moisture against the siding, which is the exact condition [Working with Wood](/library#working-with-wood) identifies as the requirement for rot. The pest half is a working rule rather than a sourced finding, but it is a widely held one in the trades: a woodpile against a wall is a sheltered, undisturbed, damp habitat with a bridge straight into the building, and the insects that like dead wood are the same ones you do not want finding your framing. **Top covered, sides open.** As above. A roof, not a bag. **Rotate it.** Burn the oldest first. A stack that never turns over grows a bottom layer that has been wet for three years and is now half compost. ## What can go wrong - **The fire will not get going and the glass sooted up overnight.** The wood is wet. Test it with a meter; do not argue with it. Nothing else on this list is nearly as common. - **You ran out in February.** Recount in cords, not in impressions. Three to ten cords a season is the range, and a face cord is a third of a cord or less. - **The wood you bought is lighter than you expected.** Either it is wetter than it should be, in which case you paid for water, or it is a lighter species than you were told, which the 10 percent identity accuracy rule gives you standing to raise. - **The chimney sweep found heavy creosote after one season.** You have been burning wet wood, damping the fire down, or both. Fix the wood first; it is the bigger of the two. - **The carbon monoxide alarm goes off, or anyone in the house has a headache that clears when they leave.** Everyone outside, then call for help from outside. Then have the flue inspected before the next fire. Do not treat a single alarm as a false alarm. - **You air sealed the house and now the stove smokes into the room on lighting.** That is backdrafting, and it is the interaction described above. Crack a window as a diagnostic, and read [Ventilation, Damp and Mould](/library#ventilation-damp-and-mould) for the real fix. - **The stack is mouldy and the bottom course is soft.** Ground contact, or a tarp over the sides. Both hold water in. - **The wood seasoned fine in summer and will not light in December.** It came back up with the weather. Cover the top and keep a week's worth indoors. - **A neighbour complained about the smoke.** They may be right, and one of EPA's at-risk groups may live there. Check whether a burn ban is in effect and whether your wood is actually dry. - **A round will not split no matter how hard you hit it.** There is a knot in your line. Move the line rather than the effort. ## You own this when - You can say how many cords your house needs for a winter, and you arrived at that by dividing an energy figure by a heat content, not by guessing. - You buy by the cord, you know a cord is 4 by 4 by 8, and you would refuse a "face cord" without asking how deep. - You own a moisture meter, you test on a freshly split face, and "under 20 percent" is a measurement rather than a hope. - Your stack is off the ground, covered on the top only, open on the sides, cut to length with the ends exposed, and away from the house. - You can explain why wet wood and a damped-down fire cause the same two problems, and name both. - Your chimney is swept and inspected every year, and you know that just under half of United States home heating fires are chimney or flue fires. - There is a working carbon monoxide alarm outside each sleeping area, you know how old it is, and you know that a wood stove in a tightened house is the specific thing that needs watching. - You did not learn felling from a document, and you stay two tree lengths from any standing tree that looks wrong. - Your firewood came from near where you burn it. When those are true you have a fuel supply rather than a pile of wood, and the understanding transfers further than firewood does. Knowing that the unit is the thing to pin down before the price, that water in a fuel is energy you have already spent, and that the failure which kills is quieter than the failure which burns are the same three habits behind every system you will ever run. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Government publications come first because they are works of the United States federal government, in the public domain, and can be redistributed with this guide. Everything after them is cited as the authority for a fact that is restated here in our own words. ### United States government (public domain) - National Institute of Standards and Technology. *Handbook 130, Uniform Laws and Regulations in the Areas of Legal Metrology and Fuel Quality*, 2026 edition, IV.B, Uniform Regulation for the Method of Sale of Commodities, section 2.4, Fireplace and Stove Wood (2.4.1.2 the definition of a cord as 128 cubic feet ranked and compactly stacked; 2.4.2 the species identity declaration and its 10 percent accuracy; 2.4.3 sale only by the cord or cubic metre and the packaged, processed and pellet exceptions; 2.4.4 Prohibition of Terms; 2.4.5 the required contents of a delivery ticket or sales invoice). https://www.nist.gov/system/files/documents/2025/12/23/2026_HB130-IV_B_Method-of-Sale-20251215.pdf - USDA Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory. *Fuel Value Calculator*, WOE-3, published with the Pellet Fuels Institute (heating values and efficiencies for green, semidried, air-dried and ovendry wood; ovendry wood at 17.2 million Btu per ton; seasoned firewood at 20 million Btu per cord gross and 15.3 million net; the statement that water commonly makes up half the weight of a living tree; latent heat of vaporisation and why that energy is not recovered; 50 to 150 million Btu to heat an average-sized home over a heating season; the annual heating cost comparison between firewood, natural gas, propane, fuel oil, pellets and electricity; the declaration that its moisture contents are on a wet basis). https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/techline/fuel-value-calculator.pdf - USDA Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory. *Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material*, FPL-GTR-190, Chapter 4, Moisture Relations and Physical Properties of Wood (moisture content expressed on the ovendry basis; equilibrium moisture content and the statement that its values may be applied to wood of any species; water absorption being most rapid in the longitudinal direction, through the end grain; the comparative thermal conductivities). https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/fplgtr/fplgtr190/chapter_04.pdf - USDA Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory. *Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material*, FPL-GTR-190, Chapter 5, Mechanical Properties of Wood, Table 5-3b (specific gravity at 12 percent moisture content for Douglas-fir Coast, western hemlock, western redcedar, red alder, bigleaf maple, black cottonwood, grand fir, Sitka spruce and lodgepole pine, and the footnote defining specific gravity as ovendry weight over volume at that moisture content). https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/fplgtr/fplgtr190/chapter_05.pdf - Environmental Protection Agency, Burn Wise. *Best Wood-Burning Practices* (wood burns best below 20 percent moisture content; season for at least six months; store outdoors off the ground with only the top covered because covering the sides traps moisture; do not burn wet or green wood; use a wood moisture meter; dry seasoned wood creates very little smoke). https://www.epa.gov/burnwise/best-wood-burning-practices - Environmental Protection Agency, Burn Wise. *Wood Smoke and Your Health* (fine particles and PM2.5 as the biggest health threat from smoke; the respiratory, asthma and cardiovascular effects; benzene, formaldehyde, acrolein and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons; the full list of groups at greater risk; the relationship between efficient burning and smoke). https://www.epa.gov/burnwise/wood-smoke-and-your-health - US Fire Administration, Federal Emergency Management Agency. *Heating Fires in Residential Buildings (2017-2019)*, Topical Fire Report Series, Volume 21, Issue 10, December 2021 (an annual average of 34,200 heating fires in residential buildings causing 165 deaths, 600 injuries and $367 million in property loss; heating as the second leading cause of all residential building fires, following cooking; the January peak at 20 percent; confined fires, specifically those confined to chimneys, flues or fuel burners, at 77 percent of residential building heating fires, and Table 2's split of that into 49.43 percent chimney or flue fires and 27.16 percent confined fuel burner or boiler malfunctions; the heat source too close to combustibles in 27 percent of nonconfined heating fires). https://www.usfa.fema.gov/downloads/pdf/statistics/v21i10.pdf - US Fire Administration. *Heating fire safety* (32,200 home heating fires in 2021 with 190 deaths, 625 injuries and $442 million in property loss; keep anything that can burn at least 3 feet from all heat sources; maintain heating equipment and chimneys by having them cleaned and inspected each year by a professional; never use an oven to heat a home). https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/home-fires/prevent-fires/heating/ - US Fire Administration. *Fireplace and Wood Stove Safety* card (3 foot clearance; do not burn paper; put the fire out before sleeping or leaving; have the chimney inspected and cleaned each year by a professional; ashes in a metal container with a lid placed outside at least 10 feet from the home; a glass or metal screen in front of a fireplace). https://www.usfa.fema.gov/downloads/pdf/publications/fireplace_woodstove_safety_card.pdf - US Fire Administration. *Carbon monoxide safety* (carbon monoxide as the invisible killer; more than 150 accidental non-fire deaths a year; alarm placement outside each separate sleeping area and on every level; keep vents for the dryer, furnace, stove and fireplace clear of snow and debris). https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/life-safety-hazards/carbon-monoxide/ - US Fire Administration. *Before a wildland urban interface fire* (keep the first 5 feet around the home clear of flammables, woodpiles named first). https://www.usfa.fema.gov/wui/outreach/before-wui-fire.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *About Carbon Monoxide Poisoning* (more than 400 deaths, more than 100,000 emergency department visits and more than 14,000 hospitalisations a year from unintentional non-fire carbon monoxide poisoning; the symptom list; have the chimney checked or cleaned every year; do not burn anything unvented on a stove or fireplace; alarm placement, battery checks at the clock change, and replacement every 5 years or per the manufacturer). https://www.cdc.gov/carbon-monoxide/about/index.html - Consumer Product Safety Commission. *CPSC Warns Of Hazards from Furnaces, Space Heaters and Fireplaces*, 2006 (have flues and chimneys inspected before each heating season for leakage and blockage by creosote or debris; about 85 deaths a year from carbon monoxide caused by heating systems, ranges and ovens, and water heaters; never close the damper or go to bed while the ashes are still warm; 3 foot clearance from flammable materials). https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/2006/CPSC-Warns-Of-Hazards-from-Furnaces-Space-Heaters-and-Fireplaces - Consumer Product Safety Commission. *CPSC Chairman Warns Of Coal And Wood Burning Stove Hazards*, 1982 (creosote described as a tarry substance condensed inside chimneys and chimney connectors; 112,000 fires involving coal and wood burning equipment in 1980). https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/1982/CPSC-Chairman-Warns-Of-Coal-And-Wood-Burning-Stove-Hazards - Consumer Product Safety Commission. *Commission Approves Mandatory Approach Toward Reducing Chain Saw Injuries From Kickback*, 1980 (the definition of kickback; an estimated 105,000 chain saw injuries requiring medical attention in 1979 of which about 24,000 were kickback injuries; the finding that a redesigned chain reduced kickback energy by as much as 74 percent). https://www.cpsc.gov/Newsroom/News-Releases/1980/Commission-Approves-Mandatory-Approach-Toward-Reducing-Chain-Saw-Injuries-From-Kickback - Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor. 29 CFR 1910.266, Logging operations (the definition of a danger tree and the requirement to fell, remove or avoid it, mark it, and keep two tree lengths clear; checking for loose bark and broken limbs before felling; chain saw leg, foot, eye and head protection; starting on the ground with the chain brake engaged, no drop starting, 10 feet from fuelling; both hands encircling the handles; shutdown or chain brake when carried over 50 feet; throttle released before retreat; the undercut, the hinge and the diagonal retreat path; the two tree length approach rule; visual or audible contact with another employee; first aid kits on site). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol5-sec1910-266.xml - USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, Plant Epidemiology and Risk Analysis Laboratory. *Risk Assessment of the Movement of Firewood within the United States*, Rev. 1, 2011 (pests surviving felling, processing and shipping; emerald ash borer needing two emergence periods and pine wood nematode surviving 20 months in chipped wood; seasoning defined as six months to a year, or three months under good conditions; spread frequently 150 to 200 miles; 8 to 57 percent of campers bringing firewood from home and travelling 100 to 200 miles; 330,000 campers moving firewood into national parks annually; 28 states with quarantine regulations and the list of organisms that prompted them; New York's 50 mile limit; heat treatment at 71.1 degrees C for 75 minutes for imports and the 60 degrees C for 60 minutes minimum for firewood; the statement that all species of trees can be and are used as firewood). https://www.aphis.usda.gov/sites/default/files/firewood_pathway_assessment.pdf - USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, Hungry Pests. *How They Spread* (do not move firewood; buy or use firewood close to where you will burn it). https://www.aphis.usda.gov/plant-pests-diseases/hungry-pests/how-they-spread - Energy Information Administration. *Increase in wood as main source of household heating most notable in the Northeast*, Today in Energy (2.5 million households, 2.1 percent, using wood as the main heating fuel, up from 1.9 million and 1.7 percent in 2005; a further 9 million households, 7.7 percent, using it as a secondary fuel; about 500 trillion Btu a year in the residential sector, about the same as propane and slightly less than fuel oil; heating stoves the most common main equipment and fireplaces the most common secondary; 2012 survey data). https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=15431 ### State agencies, cited as the authority and restated in our own words State works are not covered by 17 U.S.C. 105, so nothing below is quoted or reproduced here. - Connecticut Department of Consumer Protection. *Firewood and Stove Wood Regulations* (the list of terms a seller may not use: face cord, rack, pile, truckload or terms of similar import; the cord definition and delivery ticket contents as adopted from the model regulation). https://portal.ct.gov/DCP/Food-and-Standards-Division/Food--Standards/Firewood-and-Stove-Wood-Regulations - Puget Sound Clean Air Agency. *About Air Quality Burn Bans* (its authority over King, Kitsap, Pierce and Snohomish counties; what Stage 1 and Stage 2 burn bans prohibit and the position of certified stoves and pellet stoves in each; the approved exemption; wood smoke as a main contributor to fine particle pollution). https://pscleanair.gov/172/About-Air-Quality-Burn-Bans - Washington State Department of Ecology. *Wood stove info* (wood smoke as one of the main sources of air pollution in Washington; split, covered and stacked for at least one year, tested with a moisture meter; selling an uncertified wood stove is illegal, and removal is not required when a house is sold). https://ecology.wa.gov/air-climate/air-quality/smoke-fire/wood-stove-info ### Inside this project - [Working with Wood](/library#working-with-wood) for species properties, the fibre saturation point, decay conditions and heartwood decay classes, the Seattle outdoor equilibrium moisture content figures, and the wood dust hazard. Its numbers come from the Wood Handbook. - [Sharpening](/library#sharpening) for the axe bevel, filing direction and edge maintenance. - [Insulation and Heat Loss](/library#insulation-and-heat-loss) for the heat you are trying to keep in, and for the air sealing that makes the carbon monoxide section here matter. - [Ventilation, Damp and Mould](/library#ventilation-damp-and-mould) for the full treatment of carbon monoxide, backdrafting and alarm requirements. - [Building a Fire Staff](/library#fire-staff-materials) for the same boundary drawn around a different dangerous skill. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/species.json` for the local tree species, their uses and their status, and `data/locales/silverdale_wa/climate.json` for the monthly precipitation normals quoted here, which come from NOAA NCEI station USC00450872. ### Labelled in the text as rules of thumb or arithmetic, not as sourced values - "A year" as a seasoning time. The sourced answers range from three months to one year and disagree because the right answer depends on the wood and the weather. The meter is the answer. - Eighty cubic feet of solid wood in a 128 cubic foot cord, used to turn specific gravity into Btu per cord. The resulting figure for Douglas-fir agrees with the Forest Products Laboratory's own 20 million Btu per cord for seasoned firewood, which is why the rule of thumb is kept. - The piece lengths and the pickup bed dimensions in the unit table. The cord is defined; the rest are illustrative dimensions of mine. - Cedar throwing sparks, and a woodpile against a wall being an insect bridge into the building. Both are widely held trade knowledge and neither is sourced here. ### A note on what is not cited NFPA 211 is the standard the chimney trades actually work to, and many building codes adopt it by reference. It is copyrighted and sold, so no number in this guide comes from it. Every maintenance interval above is instead taken from a federal agency, and it is worth noticing that the US Fire Administration, the Consumer Product Safety Commission and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention independently arrive at the same annual interval for three different reasons. No chainsaw injury figure more recent than 1979 appears here. The current estimates in circulation come from analyses of the Consumer Product Safety Commission's National Electronic Injury Surveillance System published in journals this guide could not open, so they are not quoted rather than quoted second hand. EPA's Burn Wise programme ran from 2009 to 2025, and EPA states that it stopped updating the programme's content on 30 October 2025. Its pages are still the best public-domain source on firewood moisture and wood smoke, and they are cited as such, but they are now a historic record rather than a maintained one. Expect the links to move.
