docs.text: # Burns Someone has been burned. Before you read another word, the first minute matters more than anything else in this guide: 1. **Stop the burning.** Get the person away from the heat. If clothing is alight, stop them, get them on the ground, and roll them or smother the flames with something heavy. If it is electricity, the power goes off before anyone touches them. 2. **Get things off before the swelling starts.** Rings, watch, bracelets, belt, boots, and any clothing that is not stuck to the skin. Anything still stuck to the skin stays where it is. 3. **Cool the burn under running water.** Twenty minutes, cool not cold. No ice, ever. 4. **While the water is running, decide whether this needs a hospital.** The list is a few paragraphs down. If you are not sure, it does. Everything after this is the explanation. Do the four things first. One honest boundary before we go further. **This guide is not a substitute for medical care, and it does not qualify you to manage a serious burn at home.** What it can do is help you act correctly in the first minutes, tell you which burns you must hand to someone trained, and stop you doing the things that make a burn worse. Many of the remedies people reach for instinctively cause real harm, and that is the single most useful thing in here. The moment a burn is on the list of burns that need professional care, your job stops being treatment and becomes getting the person to someone who can treat it. Its companion, [Building a Fire Staff](/library#fire-staff-materials), covers the other side of this: how to build a thing that burns, and how to not get burned by it in the first place. ## Cooling: the numbers, and why ice is not a shortcut Cool running water is the whole of burn first aid. It is not a comfort measure. A systematic review in the *Journal of Burn Care & Research* covering seven studies and 11,383 patients found that people who got twenty minutes of cool running water within three hours of injury had "significantly decreased odds of requiring skin grafting or other surgical intervention." That is the difference between a burn that heals and a burn that gets operated on. The numbers: - **How long.** MedlinePlus says to keep the area under water for at least 5 to 30 minutes. The burn-care guidance summarised by CADTH is firmer, calling for at least twenty minutes for any major burn or burn over 10 percent of the body. Twenty minutes is the number to aim at. - **How cool.** The 2024 international consensus on second-degree burn wounds recommends running water between 12 and 25 degrees Celsius, roughly 54 to 77 Fahrenheit. CADTH's summary cites 15 degrees Celsius, about 59 Fahrenheit. As a rule of thumb, an ordinary cold tap is usually in that band already, which is exactly why this works without a thermometer. - **How soon.** Sooner is better, but the window is wider than people assume. The studies that found the grafting benefit measured cooling begun within three hours of injury. If you did not cool it at the time, it is still worth doing. **Ice and iced water are harmful, and this is not a small point.** The 2024 consensus is explicit about the mechanism: ice cubes are cold enough to cause "vasoconstriction of the wound blood vessels, leading to ischaemic necrosis," and also carry a risk of frostbite and hypothermia. Read that plainly. The burn has already damaged the tissue, and the blood supply is what will repair it. Ice clamps that blood supply shut. You can take living tissue at the edge of a burn and kill it with an ice pack. The CADTH summary gives the same two reasons, hypothermia and impaired blood flow, and says ice or ice water should not be used. MedlinePlus lists ice among the things never to put on a burn. There is one more wrinkle worth understanding, because it looks like a contradiction. MedlinePlus says "do not place a severe burn in cold water. This can cause shock." Both things are true. Running cool water over a burn is right. Immersing a large burn, or a whole person, in cold water is not, because burned skin loses heat fast and a cold person is a new emergency on top of the burn. Military burn guidance notes that casualties with burns over 20 percent of the body are at high risk of hypothermia and says plainly to keep the patient warm. So for a large burn: cool the burned area with running water, then cover the person and keep them warm. Cool the burn, warm the patient. ## Call for help now if any of these are true MedlinePlus says to call emergency services if: - The burn is large, about the size of your palm or bigger - The burn is full thickness - You are not sure how serious it is - The burn was caused by chemicals or electricity - The person shows signs of shock - The person breathed in smoke - Physical abuse is the known or suspected cause - There are other symptoms alongside the burn Notice the third one. "You are not sure how serious it is" is on the official list, in those words. You are allowed to not know. ## How deep is it Three depths, described by what you can actually see and feel. These descriptions come from US military burn care guidance and from the National Library of Medicine, and they agree with each other. **Superficial, also called first degree.** The outer layer of skin only. Red, painful, swollen. It does not blister, and it blanches readily, meaning the redness goes pale when you press it and floods back when you let go. Sunburn is the everyday example. **Partial thickness, also called second degree.** Outer and underlying layers. Red, moist, swollen, blistered, and it still blanches. Military guidance describes these as "moist and sensate," meaning they hurt, and they hurt a lot. A shallower partial thickness burn is red and wet and extremely painful. A deeper one turns paler, drier, mottled white, and blanches less and hurts less. **Full thickness, also called third degree.** All the layers of skin, sometimes deeper. It looks leathery and dry, white or brown or blackened. It does not blanch. And here is the thing nobody expects: > **The deepest burns can hurt the least.** Military guidance describes > full thickness burns as "insensate," and the National Library of > Medicine describes them as causing little or no pain, with skin that > may be numb. The nerve endings that report pain are in the skin. A burn deep enough to destroy them destroys their ability to complain. So "it does not hurt much" is not reassurance. On a burn that is white, leathery, dry and numb, it is the finding that tells you this is the worst kind. Two practical consequences. A big burn is usually a patchwork of all three depths, so judge the worst part, not the average. And a burn often declares itself over the first day or two, so the depth you see in the first hour is a first guess, not a verdict. ## How big is it Two methods, one for small burns and one for large. **The rule of palm.** The flat of a hand is about 1 percent of that person's body. Federal emergency medicine guidance gives the palmar hand surface as approximately 1 percent of total body surface area, stated there for a child. Published clinical teaching gives the finer version for patients generally, separating the palm alone, about 0.5 percent, from the whole hand including the fingers, about 1 percent. Use the injured person's own hand, not yours, because the whole point is that it scales with the body you are measuring, and MedlinePlus uses exactly this as the household threshold: a burn about the size of your palm or larger means call for help. **The rule of nines.** For larger burns, the body is divided into regions worth 9 percent or a multiple of it. For an adult: | Region | Percent | |---|---| | Head and neck | 9 | | Each arm | 9 | | Front of the trunk | 18 | | Back of the trunk | 18 | | Each leg | 18 | | Genitals | 1 | Those add to 100. It is a rough field estimate, deliberately coarse, and in hospital it gets refined against a proper chart. **Children are not small adults, and the rule of nines does not fit them.** Federal guidance notes that children have proportionally larger heads, up to 20 percent, and smaller legs, 13 percent in infants. This is one of several reasons a child's burn is not something to size up by eye at home. **The counterintuitive rule: superficial burns do not count.** Military guidance states that first degree burns are not included in the estimate of burn size at all. Only partial thickness and full thickness are counted. So a whole sunburned back is a 0 percent burn by this measurement, which sounds absurd until you realise that what is being measured is how much skin has stopped working, and a first degree burn has not stopped working. **The size thresholds that matter.** The American Burn Association is the authority here, and its criteria are copyrighted, so this is a summary in our own words rather than their text. A published consensus study that updated those criteria, in the *Journal of Burn Care & Research*, puts the transfer thresholds at full thickness burns over 5 percent of the body, and partial thickness burns over 10 percent. Below those, it still recommends outpatient burn referral rather than nothing, and recommends specialist consultation for any burn that might be deep, at any size. Translated for a household: a partial thickness burn bigger than about ten palms, or any full thickness burn bigger than about five, is a hospital problem. In practice you will not be measuring. MedlinePlus gives the household version, which is that one palm or larger means call. ## The burns that need professional care whatever their size Size is only one of the reasons a burn goes to a specialist. These go regardless of how small they look. The list is drawn from the American Burn Association's referral criteria, restated here, and from the published consensus study that updated them. - **Face.** Also because of what it implies about the airway. - **Hands.** Scarring across a hand costs function permanently. - **Feet.** - **Genitals and perineum.** - **Anything over a joint**, for the same reason as hands. Healing burn tissue contracts as it matures, and a contracture across a joint locks it. - **Circumferential burns**, meaning a burn that goes all the way around a limb, a finger, the neck, or the chest. Military guidance explains why: a deep circumferential burn to an arm or leg can act "like a tourniquet, reducing arterial circulation," and around the chest it can physically stop the ribcage expanding. The burned skin is stiff, the limb underneath swells, and the pressure has nowhere to go. This needs a surgeon, sometimes urgently. - **Every chemical burn.** The consensus criteria say all chemical injuries should be cared for in a burn center. - **Every electrical burn.** High voltage and lightning injuries go straight in; even low voltage injuries warrant follow-up, because some of the damage shows up late. - **Any inhalation injury**, or a good reason to suspect one. - **Burns in young children and in older adults.** The published criteria treat both groups as benefiting from specialist involvement beyond what the size thresholds alone would trigger, and the American Burn Association's guidance is that paediatric burns generally warrant referral. As a rule of thumb for a household: have a child's burn or an older person's burn looked at even when you would shrug off the same burn on yourself. The reasons are real. The same patch of skin is a bigger fraction of a smaller body, older skin is more fragile, and older adults are already the group most at risk around fire. The US Fire Administration recorded adults aged 65 and over as having 2.5 times the risk of dying in a fire compared with the population as a whole in 2020. - **Any burn on someone with other significant health problems**, or who was injured in some other way at the same time. ## Smoke, enclosed spaces, and why the airway comes first A burn that happened in an enclosed space is an airway emergency until proven otherwise, even if the skin looks fine. The blunt number, from MedlinePlus: "Over half of deaths from fires are due to inhalation injuries." Not the flames. The air. Three separate things are going on in a house fire or a vehicle fire or any fire in a closed room: - **Heat and smoke particles damage the lining of the airway.** Federal emergency medicine guidance notes that the lung symptoms of inhalation injury "rarely grossly manifest within first 24hrs" and generally evolve over 48 to 72 hours. Someone can walk and talk and look fine and be in serious trouble the next day. - **The airway swells shut.** The same guidance describes swelling at the vocal cords, from local injury or from the whole-body swelling that follows a large burn, which "can eventually occlude airway." Swelling in a tube that is already narrow is a race against a clock. - **The smoke poisons.** Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin and displaces oxygen. Hydrogen cyanide, released when synthetic materials burn, is described as "a potent and rapid cellular poison." Neither has anything to do with the burn on the skin. Signs worth taking seriously: the fire was in an enclosed space, soot around the nose or mouth, singed nose or facial hair, a hoarse or changed voice, a cough with black phlegm, a scratchy throat, chest tightness, shortness of breath, confusion, or drowsiness. Any of those, or just the fact that they were breathing smoke in a closed room, means emergency care now rather than a wait-and-see. MedlinePlus adds one small mechanical detail for someone with an airway burn: do not put a pillow under their head. It closes the airway further. ## What not to put on a burn MedlinePlus is unambiguous. Do not apply "oil, butter, ice, medicines, cream, oil spray, or any household remedy to a severe burn." Taking them one at a time, because knowing why makes it stick: - **Butter, oil, grease, lard.** A layer of fat over a burn holds heat against tissue you are trying to cool. It is not sterile. It has to be cleaned off before anyone can see the burn, and cleaning it off means scrubbing a wound that already hurts. The MedlinePlus sunburn guidance separately says to avoid oil-based products including petroleum jelly and butter. - **Ice and iced water.** Covered above. Vasoconstriction, ischaemic necrosis, frostbite, hypothermia. The one that people are most confident about is the one most likely to deepen the injury. - **Toothpaste.** A genuinely common practice: published surveys of burn first aid in several countries found people reaching for toothpaste, honey, oil, yogurt and aloe ahead of running water. Toothpaste is not sterile, it is mildly abrasive and alkaline, it traps heat, and it has to be removed. The research literature classes these as unsafe practices, and finds they cluster where formal first aid teaching has not reached. - **Honey, egg white, yogurt, flour, mud.** Same reasoning. Unsterile material pressed into broken skin, which then has to be picked out. - **Creams, ointments and sprays, including anaesthetic sprays.** Not on a severe burn. They obscure the wound, and MedlinePlus specifically advises against benzocaine and lidocaine products for sunburn. For a small superficial burn with unbroken skin, a plain moisturising lotion or aloe is fine; that is a different situation from a raw wound. - **Adhesive dressings directly on the burn.** MedlinePlus advises against putting adhesive bandages on an electrical burn, and generally a dressing that sticks to a burn becomes part of the problem when it comes off. - **Your own breath.** MedlinePlus says not to breathe, blow or cough on a burn. Blowing on it to cool it feels natural and puts mouth bacteria straight onto an open wound. - **Anything by mouth, if the burn is severe.** No water, no food, no painkillers, because they may need surgery. And one that is not a substance: **do not remove clothing that is stuck to the skin.** Cut around it and leave the stuck part alone. Pulling it takes skin with it. ## Blisters: leave them alone The evidence here is weaker than most people assume, and the honest summary is worth giving straight. **What to do in the moment is not in doubt.** Leave blisters intact. Military burn guidance says not to debride blisters until the patient has reached a facility with emergency medical or surgical capability. The 2024 international consensus rates preservation of the intact blister during early first aid as highly recommended. MedlinePlus says do not disturb blistered or dead skin. Every source agrees: not at home, not by you. **The reason is mechanical.** An intact blister is a sterile dressing that fits perfectly and that your own body made. The consensus describes it as a physical barrier that protects the wound and prevents bacterial colonisation, provides pain relief, and maintains the moist environment in which skin heals. **What the evidence does not settle** is what a clinician should do with a blister afterwards. The same 2024 consensus rates its own recommendation to preserve blisters as based on low-quality evidence, and separately allows removal, weakly and also on low-quality evidence, when a blister is already damaged, or is large, thin-walled, likely to burst, or badly contaminated. A randomised trial in *Medicine* comparing draining a blister with a needle against cutting the roof off concluded that neither is superior, with healing times around twelve days either way. A 2021 case report in the *Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery* states it outright: "There is no consensus for burn blister management." So the guidance to leave blisters alone is firm advice resting on modest evidence, and the argument among specialists is about a decision you are not the one making. Leave them intact, and let someone trained decide. ## Dressing it with what you have After cooling, cover the burn. The purpose is to keep it clean and keep the air off it, and that is all. MedlinePlus: cover with a dry, sterile bandage or a clean dressing, keep pressure and friction off it, and where the skin is broken an ointment is preferred so the dressing does not stick. For a major burn, cover with a dry sterile bandage if you have one or a clean cloth if you do not. Military guidance says the same thing in field terms: cover burns with loose, dry gauze or a clean sheet. The word doing the work is **loose**. A burn swells. Anything snug now will be a tourniquet in an hour. Burned fingers and toes get separated from each other with non-stick dressings so they do not heal stuck together. Elevate a burned limb above the level of the heart if you can, which reduces the swelling. A rule of thumb for having nothing: clean kitchen cling film, laid over the burn in loose sheets rather than wrapped around a limb, is widely taught as an improvised burn cover, because it is clean, it does not stick, and a clinician can see through it. That is not something a US federal source specifies, so treat it as a practical fallback. The sourced instruction remains loose dry gauze or a clean sheet. ## Infection and tetanus A burn is an open wound with its defences removed, and the infection risk runs for days after the injury. MedlinePlus lists the signs to watch for: drainage or pus from the burned skin, fever, increased pain, red streaks spreading out from the burn, and swollen lymph nodes. Red streaks in particular mean go now, not tomorrow. **Tetanus.** The CDC lists burns among the wounds that carry dead tissue and therefore tetanus risk, alongside crush injuries, fractures and frostbite. Adults are recommended a tetanus booster every ten years. For wound management the interval tightens: for a clean minor wound, a booster is indicated if the last dose was ten or more years ago, and for a dirty or major wound, including a burn, the trigger is five or more years. So a burn is a reason to check the date of your last tetanus shot, and if you cannot remember it, that itself is the answer. The CDC also notes that antibiotics are not a substitute for this. ## Chemical burns are a different problem A chemical burn keeps burning until the chemical is gone. Time under water is not comfort, it is removal. MedlinePlus gives the sequence: 1. Protect yourself first. Eye and skin protection. You are no help contaminated. 2. Get the person away from the source. 3. **Brush dry chemical powder off before any water touches it.** Brush it away from yourself and away from their eyes. 4. Remove contaminated clothing and jewellery. 5. Flush the skin with cool running water for 15 minutes or more. 6. Cover loosely with a sterile dressing or clean cloth. **The exception that matters.** Do not flush with water if the exposure involves dry lime, which is calcium oxide, or the elemental metals sodium, potassium, magnesium, phosphorus or lithium. Those react with water, and adding water makes the injury worse. **Do not try to neutralise a chemical** with an acid or an alkali unless a professional tells you to. The neutralisation reaction releases heat, so you end up adding a thermal burn to a chemical one. Call emergency services for difficulty breathing, seizures or loss of consciousness. For a chemical that was swallowed or inhaled, in the United States, Poison Control is **1-800-222-1222**, free, and staffed around the clock. Every chemical burn should be seen by a burn service. ## Electrical burns are a different problem again With electricity, the visible burn is often the least of it. **Before you touch anyone.** MedlinePlus says not to get within 20 feet, about 6 metres, of someone being electrocuted by high-voltage current until the power is confirmed off. For household current, unplug it, pull the fuse, or throw the breaker. If you cannot cut the power, push them clear with something non-conducting and dry, a wooden broom handle or a rubber mat, never metal and never anything wet. **Then check breathing and pulse.** Electricity kills mainly by stopping the heart. If they are unconscious with no pulse, start CPR. **Why a small electrical burn is not a small injury.** Current enters at one point and leaves at another, and it cooks tissue along the path in between. Military burn guidance is explicit that with high voltage injuries, above 1,000 volts, "skin contact points (cutaneous burns) of limited extent can hide extensive soft-tissue damage." MedlinePlus puts it plainly: some electrical burns look minor but there may be serious internal damage, especially to the heart, muscles or brain. One sign worth knowing, from the same military guidance: muscle destroyed by current releases its contents into the blood, which damages the kidneys, and the visible clue is **urine that is red or brown**. That is an emergency finding. Call emergency services for any electrical injury, including the ones that look trivial. MedlinePlus adds: no ice, no ointments, no adhesive bandages, do not break blisters or remove dead skin, and do not move the person unless they are in ongoing danger. ## Pain Ordinary over-the-counter painkillers are appropriate for minor burns. MedlinePlus recommends them for minor burns and names ibuprofen for sunburn. Follow the label, respect the dosing, and ask a pharmacist if anything about the person makes you unsure. Cool running water is itself a good analgesic, which is one more reason the twenty minutes is worth doing properly. Two limits. Do not give anything by mouth if the burn is severe, because they may need an anaesthetic. And avoid anaesthetic sprays and creams containing benzocaine or lidocaine, which MedlinePlus advises against. If pain is poorly controlled despite sensible painkillers, that is itself one of the American Burn Association's reasons to get a burn service involved. ## What healing actually looks like So you know what is normal and what is not. **A superficial burn** is red, warm and sore, and it settles over a few days. With sunburn, MedlinePlus notes the first signs may not appear for a few hours and the full effect may take 24 hours or longer, pain is worst somewhere between 6 and 48 hours, and peeling arrives several days in. Peeling is the burn resolving, not an infection. **A partial thickness burn** blisters, weeps, and is very painful for the first days. The 2024 international consensus gives the healing times by depth: a superficial second degree burn heals in under two weeks, a shallower deep one in two to three weeks, and a deeper one mostly takes longer than three weeks. Those weeks are the reason depth matters. A burn still open after about three weeks is the kind that scars badly and is usually better off surgically treated, which is why a burn that is not clearly healing by then needs review. **A full thickness burn** does not heal from the middle, because there is nothing left in the middle to heal from. It closes from the edges, slowly and with scar tissue, which is why these are grafted. What to expect along the way: swelling that peaks in the first day or two, weeping that gradually dries, itching as it heals, and skin that stays pink, tight and sensitive for months and burns easily in the sun. Keep new skin covered from sunlight. What is not normal: increasing rather than decreasing pain after the first day or two, spreading redness, red streaks, pus, a smell, fever, or a burn that has not closed within about three weeks. Any of those, get it seen. ## How you know you got it right - You stopped the burning before you did anything else. - Rings, watch and non-stuck clothing came off before the swelling did. - Cool running water ran over it for twenty minutes, and nothing colder than a tap went near it. - You covered the person up and kept them warm while you cooled the burn. - You looked at where the burn is, not just how big it is, and you know that face, hands, feet, genitals, joints, anything circumferential, anything chemical or electrical, and any burn in a child or an older adult goes to a professional whatever its size. - Nothing went on the burn except water and a loose clean covering. - Blisters are intact. - You asked when their last tetanus shot was. - If someone was in a closed space with smoke, they were seen by a clinician even though their skin looked fine. The one that carries the most weight is the fifth. Almost all of burn first aid is a short, known procedure that anyone can do. The skill that actually matters is recognising the burn that is past you, and handing it over before you have made it worse trying to help. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot. ### United States government (public domain) - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Burns (burn degrees and appearance, cooling duration, the complete do-not list, when to call 911, dressings, infection signs, prevention). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000030.htm - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Chemical burn or reaction (brushing off dry chemicals, flushing duration, the dry lime and elemental metal exception, not neutralising, Poison Control). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000059.htm - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Electrical injury (the 20 foot rule, cutting power, CPR, hidden internal damage, what not to apply). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000053.htm - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Inhalation injuries (over half of fire deaths are due to inhalation injury; symptoms). https://medlineplus.gov/inhalationinjuries.html - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Sunburn (onset and progression, peeling, pain timing, avoiding oil-based and anaesthetic products). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/003227.htm - US Department of Defense, Joint Trauma System. Burn Care Clinical Practice Guideline, CPG ID 12, version 1.3, 10 June 2025 (burn depth definitions and blanching, superficial burns excluded from size estimates, do not debride blisters before reaching a facility, loose dry gauze or clean sheet, hypothermia risk above 20 percent body surface area, circumferential burns acting as a tourniquet, high voltage injury hiding soft tissue damage, red or brown urine). https://jts.health.mil/assets/docs/cpgs/Burn_Care_CPG_10_June_2025_ID12_v1.3.pdf - US Department of Health and Human Services, Radiation Emergency Medical Management (REMM). Burns (burn depth appearance, the Rule of Nines percentages, palmar surface as approximately 1 percent, larger heads and smaller legs in children, inhalation injury evolving over 48 to 72 hours, airway occlusion, carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide). https://www.remm.hhs.gov/burns.htm - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. About Tetanus (burns among wounds carrying tetanus risk). https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/about/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Tetanus vaccination (adult booster every 10 years). https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/vaccines/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Clinical guidance for tetanus (the 10 year and 5 year wound management intervals; antibiotics are not a substitute). https://www.cdc.gov/tetanus/hcp/clinical-guidance/index.html - US Fire Administration, Federal Emergency Management Agency. Older adults and fire safety (2.5 times the fire death risk for adults 65 and over, 2020). https://www.usfa.fema.gov/prevention/home-fires/at-risk-audiences/older-adults/ ### Peer-reviewed literature - Ji, S., Xiao, S., Xia, Z., Chinese Burn Association Tissue Repair of Burns and Trauma Committee, and Cross-Straits Medicine Exchange Association of China. Consensus on the treatment of second-degree burn wounds (2024 edition). *Burns & Trauma*, volume 12, 2024, tkad061 (running water at 12 to 25 degrees Celsius for no less than 20 minutes within 3 hours; ice causing vasoconstriction, ischaemic necrosis, frostbite and hypothermia; preserving intact blisters and the limits of that evidence; healing times by depth; removing rings and bracelets). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10858447/ - Singer, Y.M., et al. Effect of 20 minutes of cool running water within 3 hours on burn patient outcomes: a systematic review. *Journal of Burn Care & Research*, 2023 (seven studies, 11,383 patients, significantly decreased odds of requiring skin grafting or other surgical intervention). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10464582/ - Bettencourt, A.P., Romanowski, K.S., Joe, V., et al. Updating the Burn Center Referral Criteria: Results From the 2018 eDelphi Consensus Study. *Journal of Burn Care & Research*, volume 41, issue 5, 2020, pages 1052 to 1062 (transfer thresholds of full thickness above 5 percent and partial thickness above 10 percent of total body surface area; anatomical sites; all chemical injuries; high voltage and lightning; children and older adults; consultation for any potentially deep burn). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7510842/ - Ro, H.S., Shin, J.Y., Sabbagh, M.D., Roh, S.G., Chang, S.C., and Lee, N.H. Effectiveness of aspiration or deroofing for blister management in patients with burns: a prospective randomized controlled trial. *Medicine (Baltimore)*, 2018 (neither aspiration nor deroofing superior; healing around twelve days either way). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5944508/ - Gupta, S., Chittoria, R.K., Chavan, V., et al. Role of burn blister fluid in wound healing. *Journal of Cutaneous and Aesthetic Surgery*, 2021 ("There is no consensus for burn blister management"). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8611715/ - Solak, M. First aid practices about wounds and burns in rural areas. *BMC Research Notes*, 2025 (34.1 percent used traditional first aid practices such as honey, oil and yogurt). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12548283/ - La Ramba, H., et al. Local understandings of burn first aid. *Acta Medica Philippina*, 2026 (first aid based on toothpaste, honey or aloe vera, while running water was rarely mentioned). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13233781/ - Alsiaghi, Y.A., et al. Community knowledge of burn first aid. *International Wound Journal*, 2026 (applying honey or toothpaste and improper handling of chemical or electrical injuries classed as unsafe practices). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13042722/ ### Health technology assessment - Canadian Agency for Drugs and Technologies in Health. Cooling for Thermal Burns: Clinical Effectiveness and Guidelines, 2019 (at least 20 minutes for any major burn or burn over 10 percent of total body surface area; running cool water at 15 degrees Celsius; ice or ice water should not be used due to the risk of hypothermia and impaired perfusion). https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK541209/ ### Copyrighted authorities, cited but not reproduced The text of these is under ordinary copyright. Every statement drawn from them above is written in our own words. - American Burn Association. Guidelines for burn patient referral (the referral criteria: anatomical sites, all chemical injuries, high and low voltage electrical injuries, suspected inhalation injury, paediatric burns, comorbidities, poorly controlled pain). https://ameriburn.org/burn-care-team/resources/guidelines-for-burn-patient-referral - StatPearls, via the NCBI Bookshelf. Burn Evaluation and Management (the palm alone at approximately 0.5 percent of body surface area against the whole hand including fingers at approximately 1 percent; full thickness burns causing little or no pain). Distributed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, so cited rather than copied. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430741/

docs.title: Cold and Hypothermia
headings: Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead
Rewarming: what helps and what harms
Wet feet, which is the injury that actually happens in a wet climate
Wind chill, and what the chart actually says
Prevention, which is where the real gains are
Copyrighted authorities, cited but not reproduced
docs.text: # Cold Someone is cold and not acting right. Before you read another word: 1. **Get them out of the wind and out of the wet.** A building, a vehicle, a tent, the lee side of anything. Wind and wet are what turn survivable cold into hypothermia, and neither of them stops while you think. 2. **Get the wet clothes off and dry cover on.** CDC's order is: warm shelter, remove wet clothing, warm the centre of the body, which means chest, neck, head and groin. Not the hands. Not the feet. 3. **Get them off the ground.** The National Park Service says to "Insulate the body from the ground using any material available such as clothing, space blanket, etc." As a **rule of thumb**, ground takes heat out of a person faster than air does; the sourced part is the instruction, and what it means in practice is that a casualty lying on cold ground with blankets piled on top is still losing. 4. **Handle them gently, and do not let them walk.** This is the one that is not obvious and the one that kills. It is explained two sections down. Move them slowly, keep them flat, do not let them walk it off, do not rub them. 5. **Call for help.** MedlinePlus says to call 911 if the person is confused or has trouble thinking. CDC says a body temperature below 95 F (35 C) needs medical attention immediately. Everything after this is the explanation. Do those five things first. One honest boundary. **This guide is not a substitute for medical care, and nothing in it qualifies you to manage severe hypothermia on your own.** Severe hypothermia is an intensive-care problem. What a person without training can genuinely do is stop the heat loss, avoid the handful of instinctive actions that make things worse, and get the casualty to people who can rewarm them properly. That is not a small job. Done right it is most of the outcome. Two companions carry parts of this subject, so they are not repeated here. Cold water is its own emergency on a much faster clock, and [Reading the Tide](/library#reading-the-tide) covers cold shock, the gasping reflex and the 1-10-1 rule in full. The cold dark house after a windstorm, and the carbon monoxide deaths that come from trying to heat it, are in [The Hazards Your Place Actually Has](/library#the-hazards-where-you-live). ## What you can actually see Hypothermia is defined by core temperature, and you will not have a core temperature. You will have a person in front of you. So here it is by what you can observe. **The shivering stage.** NIOSH lists the early symptoms as shivering, fatigue, loss of coordination, and confusion and disorientation. CDC's list for adults is shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness. For infants, CDC says "bright red, cold skin" and very low energy, which is worth knowing because a baby does not shiver the way an adult does. Shivering is the body working. It is a good sign in the sense that the furnace is still lit. It is a bad sign in the sense that the furnace should not have needed to light. **The umbles.** The National Park Service teaches the four signs with a mnemonic: "The four main signs of hypothermia can be easily remembered using the mnemonic device 'umbles'. These signs include: stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, and grumbles." The same guide notes that "These signs indicate changes in motor coordination and levels of consciousness." That is the most useful field test there is, because you do not need equipment for it. Can they walk a straight line, speak clearly, work a zip or a buckle, and hold a civil conversation? Losing any of those is a neurological sign, and a neurological sign means the cold has reached the brain. **Denial belongs on the symptom list.** Point Reyes National Seashore puts it plainly: "Victims of hypothermia often deny that they are cold and often attempt to reassure others that they are 'Okay.'" Rocky Mountain National Park adds that someone with hypothermia "is not aware of their condition because symptoms begin gradually and their confused state hinders self-awareness." So the patient's own report is the least reliable evidence you have. Trust the umbles over the reassurance. **The stage where shivering stops.** This is the one people misread. NIOSH's late symptoms are: no shivering, blue skin, dilated pupils, slowed pulse and breathing, loss of consciousness. MedlinePlus phrases it as "Shivering that cannot be controlled (although at extremely low body temperatures, shivering may stop)." Read that again with the person in front of you. They were shivering violently. Now they are calm and still. Nothing improved. The body ran out of the fuel and the nerve signalling that shivering needs, and it gave up on the one defence it had. **Shivering stopping is a deterioration, not a recovery**, and it is the moment the problem becomes an emergency rather than a discomfort. The published staging behind this, for context rather than for you to apply: the Swiss system used in the clinical literature runs from HT I, "Conscious, shivering," through HT II, "Impaired consciousness; may or may not be shivering," to HT III, "Unconscious; vital signs present," and HT IV, "Apparent death; vital signs absent." Note that the staging the professionals use is also built on what can be observed, because they cannot measure a core temperature in a snowdrift either. StatPearls places the loss of shivering at a core temperature of about 30 to 32 C. **Paradoxical undressing.** At some point in deep hypothermia, some people take their clothes off. It is real and it is common enough to have been counted. A study of 207 fatal hypothermia cases in a sub-arctic region found "Some degree of paradoxical undressing was documented in 63 of 207 (30%) cases," most often shoes, then upper body clothing, then lower. The authors attribute it to "a combination of vasodilatation with consequent skin-warming, and diminished mental capacity," reasoning that "a sudden opening of previously constricted peripheral vessels could induce a sense of warmth, and, hence, a desire to undress." Two practical consequences. If you find someone cold and partly undressed, do not assume assault or intoxication as the explanation and do not let that assumption slow the rewarming. And if someone you are with starts shedding layers in the cold and telling you they feel hot, that is not them warming up. That is a late sign. ## Nobody is dead until they are warm and dead This is the single most counterintuitive fact about cold, it is real clinical guidance rather than folklore, and the federal sources say it in plain words. MedlinePlus: **"Do not assume that someone found lying motionless in the cold is already dead."** CDC's winter weather guidance says the same thing operationally: give CPR and keep giving it, because people who appear dead from hypothermia have been revived. The clinical reasoning is in the 2021 international update on accidental hypothermia. In a hypothermic patient, "rigidity (apparent rigor mortis) is not a reliable sign of death." And the list of findings that do **not** rule out resuscitation is remarkable: "asystole, unwitnessed CA, low core temperature, long no-flow or low-flow time, fixed, dilated pupils, hypocapnia, old age, or trauma (even major trauma)." Every one of those is something a bystander, and for that matter a paramedic, would ordinarily read as death. Cold slows the metabolism of the brain and heart enormously. That is the same effect that surgeons deliberately induce for some operations. A person cooled to the point of apparent death may have an intact brain that is simply running very slowly, and that brain can come back. What this means for you: **start CPR and keep going.** The decision that someone cold is beyond help belongs to a clinician who has rewarmed them, not to you at the scene and not to the first responder either. The guidance does list genuine stopping conditions, such as a valid do-not-resuscitate order or clear signs of irreversible death like fixed dependent lividity, but those are deliberately narrow and none of them is "they look dead." ## Why gentle handling matters A severely hypothermic heart is electrically unstable. Move it roughly and it can go into a fatal rhythm. The clinical term for this is rescue collapse, and the 2021 update defines it as "Cardiocirculatory collapse during extrication or transfer of hypothermic patients," attributed "most frequently, by mechanical stimuli such as sudden movement." The scale of it: **"rescue collapse appears to double the risk of death in severely hypothermic patients."** The instruction that follows is "Patients should be transported gently and horizontally to avoid triggering hypothermic CA." A 2003 review in CMAJ gives the same instruction from the arrhythmia angle: "Because of the risk of arrhythmia, patients should have cardiac monitoring and should be transferred gently." The National Park Service gives the plain-language version: "Be gentle. Sudden movements can cause severe pain." So: no shaking them awake. No hauling them upright. No slinging them over a shoulder. No jogging them to the truck. Keep them flat. If they cannot walk, "A patient who is unable to walk, should be placed in a horizontal position on a stretcher." And do not let them exercise their way warm. Walking generates heat, but "Walking increases heat production but increases afterdrop." The 2021 guidance is that a hypothermic patient found lying down should not be allowed to walk until they have taken calories and been allowed to shiver for about 30 minutes. ## Rewarming: what helps and what harms **Afterdrop** is the thing that makes rewarming counterintuitive. When a body gets cold, it shuts blood out of the arms and legs to protect the core, and those limbs get very cold. The 2021 update describes what happens next: "After extrication from a cold environment, cooling continues by redistribution of the heat from the warm core to the cold periphery." The CMAJ review says it more briefly: an afterdrop "may occur when blood supply to the cold periphery is recirculated to the core." In other words, the limbs are a reservoir of cold blood. Open them up and that cold blood comes back to the heart, and the core gets colder after the rescue than it was during it. That single mechanism explains almost every rewarming error. **A hot bath is wrong.** It dilates every peripheral vessel at once, which is the fastest possible way to flush cold blood into an unstable heart. MedlinePlus is direct: "Do not use direct heat (such as hot water, a heating pad, or a heat lamp)." The Park Service guidance says direct heat "can do extreme damage to the skin" and to use slow methods instead. **Rubbing the limbs is wrong**, for the same reason plus a second one. It drives cold blood back to the core, and on frostbitten tissue it physically destroys cells. The military guidance for cold injury is explicit: "Rubbing the affected areas is to be avoided as this will further traumatize the skin." **Alcohol is wrong**, and the reason is worth knowing because the folklore is so strong. The CMAJ review sets out three separate mechanisms: "Alcohol and sedative drugs dull mental awareness of cold and impair the judgement necessary to seek shelter or put on warm clothing. In addition, alcohol inhibits shivering, perhaps by causing hypoglycemia, and causes cutaneous vasodilatation, which counteracts the thermoregulatory response." So it stops you noticing, stops you shivering, and opens the vessels that were protecting your core. The feeling of warmth is the heat leaving. CDC, NIOSH, MedlinePlus and the Park Service all say the same thing in one line: do not give alcohol. **What does help**, from CDC and NIOSH, in this order: - Get them somewhere warm and dry. - Remove wet clothing. - Warm the centre of the body first: chest, neck, head and groin. An electric blanket if you have one, or skin-to-skin contact under loose dry layers of blankets, clothing, towels or sheets. - If they are conscious and alert, warm drinks help. Not alcoholic, and nothing by mouth for someone who is not fully awake. - Once they are warming, keep them dry and wrap the whole body including the head and neck. - If there is no pulse, start CPR. Notice that the warming is aimed at the trunk. The CMAJ review explains why heat goes "to the trunk rather than the extremities" in exactly the afterdrop terms above. Heat packs, where used, go on the trunk and should not be put directly against skin. The recurring beginner's instinct is to warm the parts that feel coldest and complain loudest, which are the hands and feet. Those are the last parts to warm, not the first. ## Wet feet, which is the injury that actually happens in a wet climate In a mild marine climate, frostbite is rare and non-freezing cold injury is not. It gets the most space here for that reason. **Trench foot, also called immersion foot, does not require freezing and barely requires cold.** NIOSH states that it "can occur at temperatures as high as 60 F if the feet are constantly wet." Sixty Fahrenheit is about 15.6 C. That is an ordinary autumn afternoon, and that is the point. The military guideline is blunt about the cause: it is "a syndrome related to prolonged exposure to moisture. Classically it has been associated with cold water, but can happen in all climates." The timing matters: "The syndrome generally happens slower in warm water, taking approximately 48 hrs, than cold water (earliest estimate 12 hours)." Twelve hours of cold wet feet is one long day of work in the rain. **What it looks like**, from the same guideline: it begins as "water logging of the feet, most pronounced in the soles." Then, with continuing exposure, "the foot becomes hyperemic, mottled, painful and edematous, gradually progressing into blistering, hypoperfusion, ulceration and gangrene." NIOSH's symptom list is the practical version: reddening of the skin, numbness, leg cramps, swelling, tingling pain, blisters or ulcers, bleeding under the skin, and gangrene, where "foot may turn dark purple, blue, or gray." **Treatment is not what you would guess.** For frostbite you immerse in warm water. For immersion foot you do the opposite. The military guideline: rewarming "is done by air drying at room temperature," and its quality metric for the condition is that patients "have dry heat administered." Do not soak these feet. NIOSH's field version: remove shoes and boots and wet socks, dry the feet, and "Avoid walking on feet, as this may cause tissue damage." That last one is easy to get wrong because the person can usually still walk. Walking on a foot in this state damages it further, and the damage can be permanent. **Chilblains** are the mild relative and they are worth naming so you do not mistake them for something worse. NIOSH describes them as caused by "repeated exposure of skin to temperatures just above freezing to as high as 60 F," producing redness, itching, possible blistering, inflammation, and in severe cases ulceration. Their first aid is: avoid scratching, warm the skin slowly, keep any blisters clean and covered. **Prevention is dry socks and a chance to dry out.** That is the entire intervention and it is nearly free. Spare socks in a pocket. Boots that actually keep water out. Feet out of wet boots at breaks. NIOSH's prevention list for cold work includes waterproof insulated boots and carrying extra socks, and that unglamorous line is the one that matters most in a rainy climate. ## Frostbite Frostbite is tissue freezing. It needs an air temperature well below freezing, which is why it is the rarer problem in a mild wet climate and the more likely problem on a clear cold night inland or at altitude. **Check the core before the fingers.** The military guideline is explicit that hypothermia comes first: "patients are likely hypothermic and should be warmed expediently before focusing on cold injuries of the extremities." MedlinePlus gives the same order. A warm-handed corpse is not the goal. **What it looks like, by depth.** The military guideline uses four degrees: - **First degree.** Superficial skin injury. Numbness, then pain on rewarming, redness, sometimes blue mottling, swelling, and peeling that starts around day 5. - **Second degree.** Partial thickness. Everything above plus blistering surrounded by redness and swelling, appearing around day 2. - **Third degree.** The full thickness of the skin and into the tissue beneath. Skin that is bluish to black and will not deform. Blood-filled blisters. Ulceration later. - **Fourth degree.** As above but through to bone. The area may be cold to the touch and "may feel stiff or woody." CDC's version for spotting it early: "Redness or pain in any skin area may be the first sign of frostbite," followed by "a white or grayish-yellow skin area," "skin that feels unusually firm or waxy," and numbness. The parts that go first are the nose, ears, cheeks, chin, fingers and toes. **The grade is not knowable at the time.** The military guideline warns that "The ultimate grade will not be truly known until treatment has been attempted and a period of time has passed." Do not write anyone off at the scene on the basis of how bad it looks. **Rewarming, if and only if it can be finished.** The sourced number is consistent across three of them. The military guideline: "Rapid active re-warming is done in 104-108 F (40-42 C) water for 15- 30 minutes as long as care can occur in an environment where there is no risk of refreezing." MedlinePlus: "The recommended water temperature is 104 F to 108 F (40 C to 42.2 C)," soaked for 15 to 30 minutes. The CMAJ review: "Rapid rewarming of a frostbitten extremity in a bath of water between 40 C and 42 C for 15 to 30 minutes may minimize tissue loss." That range is narrow on purpose. The military guideline explains both edges: "The temperature is important, as there is reduced effect with cooler temperatures and higher temperatures will cause burns." Use a thermometer. Water that feels comfortably hot to your hand is already too hot for tissue that cannot feel it. Expect it to hurt. The guideline notes the process "can be expected to be very painful," and that the temptation to warm slowly because it is better tolerated is a mistake, since "tissue survival is improved with rapid re-warming." **Do not thaw what may refreeze.** MedlinePlus lists among the things not to do: thaw a frostbitten area if it cannot be kept thawed. The military guideline is stronger: "It is imperative to prevent refreezing of the impacted extremity as it results in more tissue damage," and "refreezing after partial thawing will result in more severe injury." A frozen foot walked out to a road is a bad outcome. A thawed foot that refreezes on the way is a worse one. **The rest of the do-not list**, from CDC and MedlinePlus: - Do not rub or massage the area. - Do not use a fireplace, heat lamp, radiator or stove. - Do not use a heating pad or electric blanket on frostbite. - Do not walk on frostbitten feet or toes unless you have no choice. - Do not break the blisters. The heating pad item looks like it contradicts the hypothermia advice, where CDC does recommend an electric blanket. Both are right, and the difference is what you are heating. An electric blanket on the trunk of a hypothermic person warms a core that can still feel and complain. Anything hot against frostbitten tissue is being applied to skin that has lost sensation, and NIOSH gives the reason directly: affected areas "are numb and can be easily burned." A numb patient cannot tell you that you are burning them. If you want the other half of that problem, see [Burns](/library#treating-burns). ## Wind chill, and what the chart actually says Wind chill is one of the most misused numbers in weather reporting, so it is worth being precise. **What it is.** The National Weather Service defines it as "how cold people and animals feel when outside," based on "the rate of heat loss from exposed skin caused by wind and cold." It is a heat-loss index for living skin, not an air temperature. **What it is not.** From the NWS: "The only effect wind chill has on inanimate objects, such as car radiators and water pipes, is to shorten the amount of time for the object to cool. The inanimate object will not cool below the actual air temperature." Wind makes things reach the air temperature faster. It does not make them colder than the air. Your pipes do not care about the wind chill number, and neither does a thermometer. **The formula**, published by the NWS and effective 1 November 2001, is: ``` Wind Chill (F) = 35.74 + 0.6215T - 35.75(V^0.16) + 0.4275T(V^0.16) ``` where T is air temperature in Fahrenheit and V is wind speed in mph. The NWS notes it applies for temperatures at or below 50 F and wind speeds above 3 mph. **The frostbite bands.** The NWS chart shades three regions, labelled 30 minutes, 10 minutes and 5 minutes, meaning the approximate time in which exposed skin can freeze. The NWS gives one worked example in words: "If the temperature is 0 F and the wind is blowing at 15 mph, the wind chill is -19 F. At this wind chill temperature, exposed skin can freeze in 30 minutes." Reading the shading off the published chart, the coldest air temperature at which each band begins, for a few representative wind speeds: | Wind | 30 min band begins at | 10 min | 5 min | |---|---|---|---| | 5 mph | -5 F | -35 F | not reached down to -40 F | | 15 mph | 5 F | -15 F | -35 F | | 30 mph | 10 F | -5 F | -20 F | | 60 mph | 15 F | 5 F | -5 F | The shape of that table is the useful part. **Wind buys the cold a great deal of ground once you are already below freezing, and almost none above it.** Going from 5 mph to 60 mph moves the 30 minute threshold only from -5 F to 15 F, twenty degrees. But at a fixed -20 F, going from 5 mph to 30 mph moves you from skin freezing in 30 minutes to skin freezing in 5. Same air, six times the hurry. **And here is the number that matters in a mild wet climate.** Across the entire published chart, at every wind speed up to 60 mph, no frostbite band appears at any air temperature warmer than 15 F, about -9 C. Silverdale's January mean low is 2.0 C, about 35.6 F. Its coldest recorded temperature is -13.9 C, about 7 F, and its winter design temperature is -6 C, about 21 F. Those and the rest of the local setting are in [Where You Are: Silverdale, Washington](/library#silverdale-wa). So in an ordinary local winter, **frostbite is essentially off the table, and that is exactly why the wind chill number is dangerous here.** A 35 F day with a 60 mph wind, which is well inside this area's windstorm record, produces a wind chill of about 17 F by the NWS formula. Damaging winter windstorms here are near-annual and the recorded peak is 77 mph, on 14 December 2000, so this is an ordinary bad day rather than an extreme. That is a genuinely alarming-sounding number and skin still cannot freeze in it. What the wind is doing at that temperature is stripping heat out of a whole person at a rate their metabolism cannot match. The injury on offer is hypothermia, not frostbite, and the chart does not have a band for that. ## Who this actually happens to **Most hypothermia deaths are not in the wilderness.** CDC recorded 1,024 deaths attributed to excessive cold or hypothermia in the United States in 2023, with the majority in January and February and November and December, January highest at 19.9 percent. In the earlier national review covering 1999 to 2002, 4,607 death certificates carried hypothermia-related diagnoses, 49 percent of the deceased were over 65, 67 percent were male, and only 22 percent were married against 52 percent of the general population. Of those deaths, "Most deaths were not work related (63%); 23% of affected persons were at home when they became hypothermic," and an Alabama study cited in the same report found that "almost half of the hypothermia-related deaths occurred indoors." Even in a genuinely cold and outdoors-heavy setting, the picture is less like mountaineering than you would expect. In the sub-arctic series of 207 fatal cases, 93 percent were found outdoors, but "a large proportion (81/207) of events occurred within close proximity to other people and buildings," many within 500 metres of a structure. Ethanol was found in 43 percent of the victims. The mean age was 62. The population this kills is old, often alone, frequently indoors in a house that has lost its heat, and frequently within sight of help. **Who is at higher risk**, from CDC and MedlinePlus: - Older adults without adequate food, clothing or heating - Infants sleeping in cold bedrooms - People who stay outdoors for long periods, including people who are unhoused, and outdoor workers - People drinking alcohol in excess or using drugs - People with chronic illness, especially heart and circulation problems - People who are malnourished or exhausted - People taking certain medications NIOSH adds a point that transfers directly to a mild climate: "In regions unaccustomed to winter weather, near freezing temperatures are considered factors for cold stress." A place that is never very cold is a place where nobody owns the right coat. ## Prevention, which is where the real gains are **Cold plus wet plus wind is a different problem from cold.** CDC states it outright: "Hypothermia often occurs at very cold temperatures, but can occur at cool temperatures (above 40 F), if a person is wet (from rain, sweat or cold water) and becomes chilled." Forty Fahrenheit is about 4.4 C. Silverdale's mean low is under 4.4 C for five months of the year, and December and January together bring about 488 mm of rain out of an annual 1,446 mm. Read those two facts together. The local winter is a machine for producing the exact combination CDC names: not very cold, very wet, and regularly windy. That is why this guide spends more words on wet feet than on frostbite. **Cotton is the problem.** Rocky Mountain National Park: "Avoid clothing that will absorb and hold water, like cotton and jeans." Cotton holds water against you, loses its loft when wet, and then evaporates that water using your body heat. A cotton shirt under a rain jacket, soaked with your own sweat, is a cooling system you are wearing. Wool and synthetics keep some insulating value wet; cotton keeps almost none. **Layers, loose ones.** NIOSH: "Wear several layers of loose clothing for insulation," and specifically that "Tight clothing reduces blood circulation to the extremities." A tight boot is a cold foot. So the extra pair of socks that does not fit in the boot is not extra insulation, it is a circulation problem. The rest of the NIOSH list is ordinary and complete: waterproof insulated boots, a hat, protection for ears, face, hands and feet, warm locations for breaks, limits on time outside, and a bag with spare socks, gloves, hat, jacket and a thermos of something hot. **Stay fed.** Shivering is muscular work and it runs on food. MedlinePlus lists "Not enough food, drinks, or rest during cold weather" among the causes of hypothermia, in the same breath as falling into cold water. The 2021 clinical guidance treats calories as part of the recovery, saying a patient should have taken calories and shivered for about 30 minutes before being allowed to walk. **Stay hydrated.** MedlinePlus names inadequate fluids as a cause alongside inadequate food. Cold suppresses thirst and cold air is dry, so the mistake is easy. **Keep the ground in mind.** Everything in the emergency section about insulating from the ground applies before the emergency too. A bed roll without a sleeping pad, a folding chair versus a rock, a stop on wet grass versus a stop on a log: those are the same decision made in advance and for free. If you want the physics of where household heat goes and how to stop it leaving, that is a separate subject and it has its own guide: [Insulation and Heat Loss](/library#insulation-and-heat-loss). ## You own this when - Your first five actions are out of the wind, out of the wet, off the ground, gently, and call, and you can do them without reading. - You warm the chest, neck, head and groin, not the hands and feet, and you can say why. - You know that shivering stopping is a deterioration. - You would start CPR on someone cold who looks dead, and you know that the decision to stop is not yours. - You know that a hot bath, rubbing the limbs and a drink are three versions of the same mistake, and that the mistake is called afterdrop. - You would not let a hypothermic person walk to the vehicle. - You treat immersion foot by drying it in air, and frostbite by immersing it in water at 104 to 108 F, and you do not confuse the two. - You would not thaw a frozen foot you could not keep thawed. - You read a wind chill number as a rate of heat loss from a person, not as a temperature anything reaches. - You carry spare socks in the rain. The one carrying the most weight is the sixth. Almost everything on this list is knowledge. That one is a decision you will have to make while a cold, confused adult is insisting they are fine and would rather just walk, and it has to have been made in advance. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. Federal government publications are listed first because they are public domain and can be redistributed with this guide; the rest cannot. ### United States government (public domain) - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Hypothermia (definition and the 95 F threshold, symptoms including shivering stopping at extremely low temperatures, causes including inadequate food, drink and rest, first aid order, do not assume someone motionless in the cold is dead, no direct heat, no alcohol, risk groups). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000038.htm - National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus. Frostbite (appearance and progression, checking for hypothermia first, the 104 to 108 F rewarming range and the 15 to 30 minute duration, do not thaw what cannot be kept thawed, no dry heat, no rubbing, do not disturb blisters). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000057.htm - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Preventing Hypothermia, Winter Weather (warning signs in adults and infants, the below 95 F rule, the treatment order, warming the centre of the body, electric blanket and skin-to-skin, warm non-alcoholic drinks, CPR, who is at risk). https://www.cdc.gov/winter-weather/prevention/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Preventing Frostbite, Winter Weather (early signs, body parts affected, what to do, and the four do-nots: no walking on frostbitten feet, no rubbing, no fireplace or heat lamp or radiator or stove, no heating pad or electric blanket). https://www.cdc.gov/winter-weather/prevention/preventing-frostbite.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Avoid, Spot, Treat: Frostbite and Hypothermia, publication CS253565-A (hypothermia can occur above 40 F if a person is wet and becomes chilled; the at-risk list; the numbered treatment and caution steps). https://www.cdc.gov/winter-weather/media/pdf/avoid-spot-treat-frostbite.pdf - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health. Cold-related Illnesses in Workers (early and late hypothermia symptoms, frostbite first aid and why numb skin burns easily, trench foot at temperatures as high as 60 F with its symptom list and first aid, chilblains). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/cold-stress/about/related-illness.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, NIOSH. Cold and Work: Types, Causes, Preparation (the four cold-related illnesses; regions unaccustomed to winter weather; loose layers; hats; warm liquids). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/cold-stress/about/index.html - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, NIOSH. Fast Facts: Protecting Yourself from Cold Stress, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication No. 2010-115 (the same illness descriptions in compact form, plus the prevention list: loose layers, tight clothing reducing circulation, waterproof insulated boots, spare socks, chemical hot packs). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/docs/2010-115/pdfs/2010-115.pdf - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Hypothermia-Related Deaths, United States, 1999-2002 and 2005, MMWR (4,607 death certificates, 49 percent over 65, 67 percent male, 22 percent married, 63 percent not work related, 23 percent at home, the Alabama indoor finding). https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5510a5.htm - Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. QuickStats: Percentage Distribution of Deaths Attributed to Excessive Cold or Hypothermia, by Month, United States, 2023, MMWR volume 74 (1,024 deaths in 2023; January highest at 19.9 percent). https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/74/wr/mm7406a6.htm - National Weather Service. Understanding Wind Chill (the definition as how cold people and animals feel, the rate of heat loss from exposed skin, the formula, and the worked example of 0 F with 15 mph wind giving a wind chill of -19 F at which exposed skin can freeze in 30 minutes). https://www.weather.gov/safety/cold-wind-chill-chart - National Weather Service. Wind Chill Questions (inanimate objects such as car radiators and water pipes will not cool below the actual air temperature; the formula applies at or below 50 F and above 3 mph). https://www.weather.gov/safety/cold-faqs - National Weather Service. Wind Chill Chart, effective 1 November 2001 (the full temperature and wind speed matrix, and the shaded frostbite time bands of 30, 10 and 5 minutes that the table in this guide is read from). https://www.weather.gov/media/safety/windchillchart3.pdf - National Weather Service. Cold Water Hazards and Safety (cold shock, the 77 F gasping threshold, incapacitation within seconds). Used here only to point at the companion guide. https://www.weather.gov/safety/coldwater - National Park Service, Rocky Mountain National Park. Winter Ecology Teacher Guide (the "umbles" mnemonic and what it indicates; be gentle because sudden movements cause severe pain; do not apply direct heat; insulate the body from the ground; that a person with hypothermia is often unaware of their own condition). https://www.nps.gov/romo/learn/education/upload/Winter-Ecology-Teacher-Guide-for-web.pdf - National Park Service, Rocky Mountain National Park. Hypothermia (warning signs; avoid cotton and jeans; ensure a barrier between the ground and the person; warm non-alcoholic drinks; get professional help immediately). https://www.nps.gov/romo/planyourvisit/hypothermia.htm - National Park Service, Point Reyes National Seashore. Your Safety: Hypothermia (signs including fumbling hands and memory lapse; that victims often deny being cold and reassure others they are okay; get out of wind and rain; heat packs to neck, armpit and groin; never alcohol). https://www.nps.gov/pore/planyourvisit/yoursafety_hypothermia.htm - US Department of Defense, Joint Trauma System. Frostbite and Immersion Foot Care, CPG ID 59, 26 January 2017 (the four degrees of frostbite and their appearance; that the grade is not knowable until later; warm the hypothermic core before the extremities; rapid rewarming at 104 to 108 F for 15 to 30 minutes and why that range is narrow; rewarming is very painful and should not be done slowly; no rubbing; refreezing causes worse injury; immersion foot from prolonged moisture in any climate, roughly 12 hours in cold water and 48 in warm, its clinical progression, and that it is rewarmed by air drying at room temperature rather than by soaking). https://jts.health.mil/assets/docs/cpgs/Frostbite_and_Immersion_Foot_Care_26_Jan_2017_ID_59.pdf ### Peer-reviewed literature - Paal, P., et al. Accidental Hypothermia: 2021 Update. *International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health*, volume 19, issue 1, 2022, article 501 (the Swiss staging system HT I to HT IV described by observable signs; afterdrop by redistribution from core to periphery; rescue collapse and that it appears to double the risk of death in severely hypothermic patients; transport gently and horizontally; walking increases afterdrop; calories and about 30 minutes of shivering before walking; apparent rigor mortis is not a reliable sign of death; the list of findings that are not contraindications to rewarming a hypothermic patient in cardiac arrest, and the narrow list that is). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8744717/ - Biem, J., Koehncke, N., Classen, D., and Dosman, J. Out of the cold: management of hypothermia and frostbite. *CMAJ: Canadian Medical Association Journal*, volume 168, issue 3, 2003, pages 305 to 311 (the three mechanisms by which alcohol worsens cold exposure: dulled awareness and judgement, inhibited shivering, and cutaneous vasodilatation; afterdrop and why heat is applied to the trunk rather than the extremities; gentle transfer because of arrhythmia risk; frostbite rewarming at 40 to 42 C for 15 to 30 minutes). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC140473/ - Brandstrom, H., Eriksson, A., Giesbrecht, G., Angquist, K.-A., and Haney, M. Fatal hypothermia: an analysis from a sub-arctic region. *International Journal of Circumpolar Health*, volume 71, 2012, article 18502 (paradoxical undressing documented in 63 of 207 cases, 30 percent, and which garments went first; the vasodilatation and diminished mental capacity explanation; 93 percent found outdoors but 81 of 207 events close to people and buildings; ethanol in 43 percent; mean age 62). https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3417546/ ### Copyrighted authorities, cited but not reproduced The text of this is under ordinary copyright. Every statement drawn from it above is written in our own words. - StatPearls, via the NCBI Bookshelf. Hypothermia (the mild, moderate and severe core temperature bands, and that shivering typically ceases at a core temperature of about 30 to 32 C, at which point paradoxical undressing may be observed). Distributed under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, so cited rather than copied. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545239/ ### Project data - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/climate.json`. The local temperature and precipitation figures: January mean low 2.0 C, December mean low 1.7 C, December and January precipitation of 252 mm and 236 mm against an annual 1,446 mm, record low -13.9 C, winter design temperature -6 C. That file's own provenance is NOAA NCEI 1991-2020 Normals for station USC00450872 near Bremerton, with the design temperature from Bremerton National Airport. - `data/locales/silverdale_wa/hazards.json`. The near-annual winter windstorm record for the Kitsap Peninsula, including the 77 mph peak of 14 December 2000, which is where the 60 mph figure in the wind chill worked example comes from. ### Computed rather than quoted - The wind chill value of about 17 F for 35 F air with a 60 mph wind was computed here from the National Weather Service formula above, not read from a published table. The formula is valid in that range, being at or below 50 F and above 3 mph. - The frostbite band table was read off the shading of the published NWS wind chill chart rather than from a written list, because the NWS publishes the bands graphically. It reproduces the one example the NWS does state in words, 0 F with a 15 mph wind falling in the 30 minute band, which is the check that it was read correctly. ### Not sourced to any authority - **The claim that ground conducts heat out of a person faster than air does.** It is the reason every source above tells you to insulate from the ground, but none of the federal sources consulted states the physical comparison, so treat the mechanism as a **rule of thumb** and the instruction, which is sourced to the National Park Service, as the part to act on. - **The advice to carry spare socks specifically.** NIOSH's prevention list includes carrying extra socks, so the practice is sourced; the emphasis placed on it here for a wet marine climate is this guide's own judgement, drawn from the sourced fact that immersion foot needs only wet feet and about 12 hours.
