docs.text: # Sharpening: Why the Dull Blade Is the Dangerous One Most people believe a sharp blade is the hazard and a dull one is merely annoying. It is the other way round, and getting this backwards is how people end up in an emergency room. The decision you are actually making is this: **every time you pick up a cutting tool, you are choosing between spending five minutes on the edge and pushing harder than the job needs.** Pushing harder is the dangerous option. Everything below serves that one choice. Here is the mechanism, and it is not complicated. A dull edge does not start the cut. You lean on it. When it finally goes, it goes with all that stored force behind it, and it goes somewhere you did not plan, which is usually into the hand holding the work. A sharp edge starts where you put it, needs almost no push, and if it does slip it is not carrying much energy. Sharpening is therefore a safety skill first and a quality skill second. Where a number appears here it comes from a government publication or a peer-reviewed study that measured it. The best sources on this subject are unusually good: the USDA Forest Service has published detailed public-domain manuals on filing axes and crosscut saws, and the Army and Navy jointly publish a hand tool manual that is better on sharpening stones than most books you can buy. Every number traces to something in the Sources list at the bottom. Where a figure is trade practice rather than a measured value, it says so in the text. ## What the evidence actually says, and what it does not Be careful here, because the argument at the top of this page is made confidently all over the internet and the supporting evidence is partial. **The force half is measured.** Researchers instrumented knives and followed fifteen professional meat cutters through lamb shoulder boning, beef rib trimming and beef loin trimming in two packing plants. Sharper blades required statistically significantly lower peak and mean cutting moments, and lower grip forces, than dull knives. The numbers give a sense of scale: peak cutting moments reached 17.2 newton metres on shoulder boning, and grip forces averaged 28.3% of each worker's maximum voluntary contraction with peaks at 72.6%. A dull knife pushes those numbers up. That is a real measurement, not a saying. **The authority half is stated but not quantified.** OSHA's hand and power tools guidance puts it plainly: knives and scissors must be sharp, and dull tools can cause more hazards than sharp ones. The same document tells you to direct saw blades and knives away from walkways and away from anyone working near you. **The injury half is inference.** No study found for this guide directly measures injury rate against edge sharpness. What is measured is the scale of the problem: an analysis of the federal injury surveillance system found an estimated 434,259 knife-related injuries treated in United States emergency departments every year, about 1,190 a day, or 1.56 per thousand people per year. Fingers and thumbs were hurt in 66% of cases, and 94% of injuries were lacerations. The same paper opens by noting that knives cause more disabling injuries than any other type of hand tool. Pocket and utility knives accounted for 47% of the injuries where a knife type was recorded, and kitchen knives for 36%. So: the force increase is proven, the hazard claim is the position of the federal safety regulator, the mechanism is obvious, and the direct injury comparison has not been published. That is an honest summary. It is still more than enough to sharpen your tools. ## What an edge actually is An edge is not a thing added to a blade. It is a **geometric coincidence**: two surfaces meeting so precisely that the line where they meet has almost no width. That line is the **apex**. This matters because it changes what you think you are doing. You are not putting an edge on. You are **removing metal from two surfaces until they intersect cleanly**. Every stroke of every stone is subtraction. If the two surfaces do not yet meet, no amount of polishing will make them cut, and this is the single most common reason a beginner sharpens for twenty minutes and ends up with a blade that still will not cut paper. They polished two surfaces that never touched. How small is small? A straight razor is honed to a wedge with a total included angle of about 17 degrees and a tip radius of roughly 40 nanometres. Forty nanometres is smaller than many of the individual structural features inside the steel itself. That last fact is the key to how edges die. Research published in *Science* in 2020 followed razor blades cutting human hair inside an electron microscope. The blades did not simply wear smooth. They **chipped**: microscopic cracks started where the steel's internal structure varied from point to point along the edge, and a chunk of the apex broke away. The chipping happened before any appreciable wear had occurred. The authors are careful that the conditions have to line up, so it is not every stroke, but it is what took the blade out. That study is about razors and hair, so do not stretch it into a law about every blade. What it does establish is that **an edge can go from sharp to useless by fracturing rather than by rounding over**, and two practical consequences follow: - **A dull edge is often a damaged edge, not a worn one.** You may not be restoring a gently rounded curve at all. You may be cutting back past a chipped line until you reach sound metal, which takes more removal than people expect. - **Thinner is sharper and also more fragile.** The Forest Service crosscut saw manual says this about saw teeth in exactly these terms: the more pointed a tooth is filed, the deeper it sinks and the hungrier the saw is, but a sharply pointed tooth wears faster than one less sharply pointed. That trade is the whole of edge geometry, in one sentence, for every tool you own. ## The burr: your one reliable checkpoint This is the most useful thing a beginner can learn, and it turns sharpening from guesswork into a procedure with a test you can pass. When you grind one side of a blade far enough that the two surfaces finally meet, the metal at the apex has nowhere left to go. It folds over to the far side as a thin ragged lip. This is the **burr**, also called a wire edge or a feather edge. You cannot usually see it. You can feel it by sliding a fingertip **off the edge, across it, never along it**. A burr is not a defect. It is proof. **It is the only unambiguous signal that you have removed enough metal to reach the apex at that point on the blade.** No burr means the surfaces have not met yet and you are not finished, however long you have been at it. The procedure the Forest Service ax manual gives, which is the same procedure for a kitchen knife, is: 1. Work one side until **a burr can be felt along the whole length of the edge**. Not part of it. The whole length, from heel to tip. If the middle burrs and the tip does not, keep going on the tip. 2. Turn the blade over and work the other side until **the burr flips back across to the first side**, again along the whole length. 3. Move to a finer abrasive and repeat, more lightly. The burr gets smaller each time. 4. Remove the last of it, which is what stropping is for. More on that below. The ax manual is blunt about step 1: stop filing once you have filed one side so that a burr of metal can be felt on the back side, then turn the ax over and continue on the other side until the burr goes back over to the side where you started. The crosscut saw manual adds a warning worth carrying over to every tool. Remove the burr periodically as you go, because **a burr can hide the true shape of the edge** and make you think you are further along than you are. Its instruction for saw teeth is to knock the burr off with a whetstone, a light stroke of the file, or even a piece of hardwood. ## Angle: consistency beats the number The exact number matters far less than people think. Holding the same number for every stroke matters enormously, because a wobbling angle grinds a rounded shoulder instead of a flat surface, and a rounded shoulder never meets its partner at a clean apex. The Forest Service says this in the plainest possible way in its handtool manual: blade and edge bevels may vary with individual preference and with the task at hand, an ax bevel for softwoods might be thinner than one for hardwoods, and experience and experimentation will determine the right bevel for each tool and job. The crosscut saw manual says the same about saw teeth, that the consensus is less bevel on a cutter tooth for hardwood than for softwood. Read that as permission to stop agonising. Pick an angle, hold it, and adjust later if the edge chips or will not bite. The working ranges below give the total included angle where that is what the source specifies, and the per-side angle where that is the convention. Read the last column carefully. | Tool | Working angle | Where this comes from | |---|---|---| | Straight razor | About 17 degrees total | Measured, from published research on razor steel | | Kitchen knife | About 15 to 20 degrees per side | **Trade practice.** No federal source found. Softer steels and heavier work want the higher end | | Woodworking chisel or plane iron | About 25 degrees primary, often a 30 degree micro-bevel at the very tip | **Trade practice.** No federal source found | | Axe | About 25 degrees, and **slightly convex**, filed back 2 to 3 inches from the edge | USDA Forest Service ax manual, which supplies a printed gauge template | | Machete | Keep the factory bevel | USDA Forest Service handtool manual: use a mill bastard file or whetstone to maintain the factory edge bevel | | Hoe, McLeod, grub hoe | 45 degrees, outside bevel | USDA Forest Service handtool manual | | Shovel | About 45 degrees, bevel on the inside (top) face | USDA Forest Service handtool manual | | Twist drill | 118 degrees included, that is 59 degrees each side of the axis, with 8 to 12 degrees of lip clearance | US Army machine tool manual: the general purpose drill point | **Convex, flat or hollow.** The ax manual asks for a rounded, slightly convex profile and a fan shape spreading back over the cheek of the head. The handtool manual explains why: when you grind, arc the blade toward its midpoint so it ends up with a full-width convex bevel, and be careful not to hollow grind, which leaves the bevel dished to the radius of the grinding wheel. A hollow bevel is thinner just behind the apex, which is exactly where an impact tool needs steel. The crosscut manual makes the same point from the other direction: a saw tooth whose filed surface is flat develops a concave cutting edge and a thin, weak point. Short version: for anything you swing or lever, convex. For anything you push through a controlled cut, flat is fine and easier to hold. ## Abrasives, honestly Every abrasive does the same job, which is scratching metal off. They differ in how fast, how flat they stay, how much mess they make and what they cost. The Forest Service handtool manual publishes a comparison of sharpening stones with a speed rating for each. The prices are from 2005 and are useless now, so they are left out; the ranking is not. | Stone | Natural or synthetic | What it is for | Speed | |---|---|---|---| | Washita | Natural | Shaping and roughing | Fast | | Soft Arkansas | Natural | Sharpening | Medium | | Hard white Arkansas | Natural | Edge finishing | Slow | | Black hard Arkansas | Natural | Edge polishing | Very slow | | Silicon carbide | Synthetic | Roughing to sharpening | Fast to medium | | India | Synthetic | Roughing to sharpening | Fast to medium | | Crystolon | Synthetic | Roughing to sharpening | Fast to medium | | Diamond on nickel | Synthetic | Sharpening hard steels | Medium | | Silicon carbide in rubber | Synthetic | Deburring | Fast | That manual's own recommendation is **synthetic**, because synthetic abrasives are harder than natural stones, their uniform particle size gives an even surface, and they cost less. If you want a natural stone for the final polish, do the rough work on a synthetic first so you do not wear out the expensive stone on work it is not needed for. What the common types mean in practice: - **Oilstones.** Light oil floats the swarf, the metal and grit, off the surface so it does not lodge in the pores. Use oil on an oilstone. If it glazes because the pores have filled, clean it with a citrus-based solvent and a stiff brush. - **Waterstones.** Water does the same floating job. They cut fast and polish well, and the ax manual warns they are much softer than oilstones and tend to cup and wear faster. They need flattening often. - **Diamond plates.** Steel plate with diamond grit bonded to it. They stay flat, they cut hard steels that ordinary stones struggle with, and there is nothing to glaze. They are the low-fuss choice. - **Ceramic.** Very hard, very slow, almost no wear. A finishing abrasive, not a shaping one. - **Sandpaper on glass.** Wet-and-dry paper laid on a sheet of glass or a machined flat. The Forest Service uses exactly this arrangement to reshape worn stones: rub the stone over coarse sandpaper, or over glass sprinkled with carborundum powder, keeping it wet. If it will flatten a stone it will sharpen a chisel. It is cheap, it is flat, and the paper is consumable. - **Files.** For axes, mower blades, mattocks, machetes and anything else too soft and too battered to bother a stone with. A 10 inch mill bastard file is the Forest Service's all-round recommendation. **Understanding file cut.** Files are graded two ways at once and the labels confuse everyone. The pattern of teeth: **single-cut** files have one series of parallel teeth set at 60 to 80 degrees to the edge and are for finishing; **double-cut** files have two crossing series at 45 degrees to each other and are for restoring shape. The coarseness, for files of the same length: **bastard** is coarsest, then **second cut**, then **smooth**. Longer files of the same grade are coarser than shorter ones. **Grit numbers.** An abrasive grain number is a sieve mesh count: grain number 40 means the grains passed through a sieve with about 40 openings to the linear inch. Bigger number, smaller grit, finer finish. That is the definition. The specific progressions people recommend, such as 1000 then 4000 then 8000 on waterstones, are trade practice, not standards, and any three reasonably spaced grits work. **When coarse is the right answer.** This is where beginners waste the most time. If the edge is chipped, rolled, or has simply never met itself, a fine stone cannot fix it, because a fine stone removes almost no metal. More strokes on a fine stone is not equivalent to fewer strokes on a coarse one. The rule: - **No burr after a few minutes on a fine stone?** You are on the wrong stone. Drop to coarse. - **Visible chips or a rolled edge?** Coarse, or a file. - **Edge is there but not keen?** Fine, then finer. - **Edge was sharp yesterday and is merely tired?** No stone at all. See the keeping-it section. The general shape of this, as the Army and Navy tool manual describes a two-sided stone, is that the coarse face removes nicks and reshapes, and the fine face completes the job and puts a keen edge on. ## Stropping is not sharpening A strop is a piece of leather, canvas, or a block of soft clear wood. Drawing the blade **backwards**, spine first, along it does two things: it tears off the last of the burr, and it aligns and burnishes the very apex. The Forest Service ax manual gives the direction precisely: strop by drawing the ax toward the edge, the opposite of the direction used during sharpening, on finished leather or a piece of soft clear wood such as pine. The Army and Navy manual says the same about any blade, that the wire edge left by a stone may be removed by stroking both sides on a soft wood block, canvas, or leather. What a strop does **not** do is remove meaningful metal or change the geometry. If a blade will not cut, stropping will not save it. Strop after sharpening, and strop between sharpenings to keep an edge pleasant, but do not mistake it for the work. Compounds, the waxy abrasive bars sold to charge a strop with, do add a little cutting action. That is trade practice rather than a specified process, and a bare leather strop already does the job the Forest Service describes. ## Tool by tool ### Kitchen knife The easiest place to learn, because the steel is soft enough to respond quickly and the angle is forgiving. Medium stone until you raise a burr along the entire edge, flip, raise it back, go to a fine stone, strop. Hold the same angle; a guide clip or a folded matchbook under the spine is a legitimate beginner's crutch. ### Chisel and plane iron The only tools here where flatness is as important as the bevel. The back of a chisel is one of the two surfaces that form the apex, so if the back is not flat and polished near the edge, the edge cannot be sharp no matter what you do to the bevel. The usual practice, which is trade practice rather than a specification, is to flatten the back once, properly, on a coarse abrasive, and then to sharpen only the bevel from then on. ### Axe The best-documented tool in this guide, because the Forest Service wrote a manual about it. Clamp the head so both hands are free. Wear leather gloves. Fit the file with a knuckle guard, which can be made from leather, wood, a piece of fire hose, or old linen hose. File **into** the edge, toward the middle of the handle, because that creates the least burr to remove on the other side. A single-cut file only cuts on the push stroke, so lift it clear on the return; sawing back and forth loads the file with metal and ruins it. Work back 2 to 3 inches from the edge with a fan shape across the cheek, keeping the profile rounded, chasing the burr from side to side, then hone with a stone and strop. ### Machete and brush tools Keep the factory bevel with a mill bastard file or a whetstone. Repair nicks and dull spots **immediately**, before the next use, and do not work with a dull or defective brush tool at all, because a brush tool that skates off a springy stem goes somewhere unpredictable at swing speed. ### Scissors and shears Sharpen, do not grind. The Army and Navy manual is specific and useful here: dull shears can usually be sharpened on an oilstone or with a file; do not grind them if sharpening is all that is needed, because **most shears become useless after two or three grindings**. Grind only if the edges are actually nicked, damaged or distorted. And never touch the flat inside faces, because two scissor blades cut by shearing past each other and that contact plane is the mechanism. ### Drill bit Sharpenable by hand on a grinder, with practice, to 118 degrees included with 8 to 12 degrees of clearance behind each lip. Both lips must come out the same angle and the same length. The Army manual spells out what happens otherwise: if the lip angles differ, only one lip cuts as the drill revolves, the hole comes out oversized, and the drill wears very rapidly. A drill point gauge, set at 59 degrees, removes the guessing, and the manual says to use it frequently to check both lip angle and lip length. This is the tool most likely to be ruined by heat, so read the temper section below before trying. ### Saw Depends entirely on which saw. A traditional handsaw is sharpenable with a triangular file and is a reasonable second-year skill. A crosscut felling saw is a trade in itself: the Forest Service manual walks through cleaning, hammering out kinks, jointing the teeth to a circle, fitting and swaging the rakers, pointing up the cutter teeth, and setting the teeth to about 0.010 inch for a felling saw or 0.015 inch for a heavy bucking saw, each step with its own gauges. Two saws you cannot sharpen at all, and this is **trade knowledge** rather than anything sourced here: a modern hardpoint handsaw has hardened teeth and is sold as a consumable, and a carbide-tipped circular blade needs diamond wheels and a machine. For any saw, the Army and Navy manual's maintenance advice still applies: never cut nails or other metal with a woodcutting saw, do not force a saw that binds but spread the cut with a wedge, and touch up the teeth with a file occasionally rather than waiting until it will not cut. ### What a beginner should not attempt yet Only the shears entry below comes from a manual. The rest is judgement, offered as trade practice. - **Crosscut and bandsaw blades.** Not because they are dangerous to sharpen, but because a badly filed saw is worse than a dull one and you will not know which mistake you made. Learn from a person. - **Scissors and shears you care about.** See above. The material budget is two or three grindings for the life of the tool. - **Carbide anything.** Wrong abrasive, wrong machine. - **Serrated knives.** Each scallop needs a tapered rod of the right diameter, and the flat side must never be ground. - **Reshaping a good chisel or plane iron on a dry bench grinder.** The next section explains why. ## Testing sharpness, safely **Do not run a thumb or finger along the edge.** It is the commonest test and it is how people cut themselves while checking whether they might cut themselves. Three tests that do not require touching the apex with soft tissue: - **The light test.** Look straight down into the edge with a light over your shoulder. A properly honed edge has no flat at the apex, so there is nothing to reflect, and **it reflects no light**. Any bright line or bright dot is a flat spot or a nick. The Forest Service ax manual uses exactly this test, and notes that a single point of light is usually a ding that will disappear over several sharpenings and need not be chased. - **The fingernail test.** Rest the edge lightly **across** your thumbnail, not along it, and try to slide it. A sharp edge bites in and stays. A dull one skates. The ax manual gives this as the safer alternative to the traditional test of shaving hair off the back of the hand, and calls it equally effective. - **Cutting something.** Paper held by one corner, or a tomato skin, or for a woodworking edge a slice of end grain in softwood. If it needs a push, it is not sharp. ## Keeping it, which is most of the work Sharpening is the small part. Nearly all edge life is decided by what happens in between. **A steel or ceramic rod is not a sharpener.** A rod realigns an edge that has rolled over rather than removing metal to make a new one. That distinction is trade practice rather than a measured specification, but the working consequence is solid: a rod restores an edge that is tired, and does nothing for one that is chipped or genuinely blunt. Ten seconds on a rod before each use, and a real sharpening when the rod stops helping. **What ruins edges.** The mechanism in each row is just relative hardness or repeated impact. The ordering is judgement about ordinary domestic use, not data. | Cause | What it does | |---|---| | Cutting on glass, stone, ceramic or steel | Chips the apex outright. These are all harder than blade steel | | Cutting down onto a plate | Same, in miniature, every meal | | Cutting through bone, staples, nails or wire | One impact, one chip | | Letting blades touch each other in a drawer | Random nicks along the whole edge | | Dishwashers | Heat, alkaline detergent and knocking about | | Rust | Pits the apex, which is the thinnest and most exposed metal | Cutting boards of wood or soft plastic, and never on a plate, is the single largest change most people can make. Which board material is kindest to an edge is trade practice and not something this guide can source, but the general rule that a surface harder than your steel will chip your steel is simply hardness. **Storage** should stop the edge touching anything hard. A sheath, a block, a magnetic bar, an edge guard. The Forest Service, the Army and the Navy all say some version of the same thing: protect sharpened edges at all times, store to protect the cutting edge, coat metal with light oil for long storage, and never store a saw in a wet sheath. **Two conditions worth knowing.** The Army and Navy manual warns that in very cold weather a chopping tool should not be used before the blade is warm, because a cold blade is brittle and will break easily. And a rusty tool is a dull tool, because rust attacks the thin metal at the apex first. ## Safety ### The injuries sharpening itself causes Sharpening puts your fingers next to a freshly sharpened edge on purpose, repeatedly, for an extended period. The four defences, all from federal manuals: - **Gloves.** Wear leather gloves throughout, on both hands. The ax manual is explicit that this is because the blade becomes razor-sharp during the process, and the handtool manual repeats it for all filing. - **A file guard.** A knuckle guard on the file keeps your fingers off the edge when the file skips, which it does. Leather, wood, a piece of fire hose or old linen hose all work. - **Secure the tool, free both hands.** Clamp the head to a bench at a comfortable height, or wedge it. Holding a tool in one hand and a file in the other is how the file slips. - **Choose the stone that does not put fingertips in the path.** The ax manual notes that traditional round pocket stones can be dangerous because your fingertips are always in jeopardy, and that the version with a finger groove in the middle exists precisely to fix that. ### Which way to stroke **Always cut away from the body.** The Army and Navy manual gives that rule for knives with a single named exception, the draw knife, which is designed to be pulled. OSHA's guidance adds the other half: direct saw blades, knives and other tools away from walkways and away from anyone working near you. Sharpening has its own directions, and they are not the same: - **Filing an axe:** file **into** the edge, because it raises the least burr. - **Using a stone on a blade:** stroke with **the sharp edge trailing**, in a circular motion, light even pressure. - **Stropping:** draw the blade **backwards**, spine first, away from the edge. - **A wet pedal grindstone:** rotate it **toward you and into the blade**. ### Power grinders A bench grinder is the fastest way to reshape a damaged tool and the fastest way to destroy one. Both federal regulation and the shop manuals converge on the same short list. - **Eye protection, always.** The Army machine tool manual calls eye protection the most important safety rule in the shop and specifies safety glasses with side shields, with goggles worn over prescription glasses. The Army and Navy hand tool manual's warning on bench grinders is to wear eye protection and watch the fingers, and to hold the work firmly so it cannot catch in the wheel. The Forest Service adds heavy leather gloves, long sleeves and a leather apron against sparks and hot shavings, plus shields and hood guards on the grinder itself. - **Ring test every wheel before you mount it.** Tap it gently with a light non-metallic implement. A ringing note means sound. A dull note means cracked, and OSHA says a wheel that sounds dead shall not be used. - **Check the speed.** OSHA requires the machine's spindle speed to be verified before mounting, so it cannot exceed the maximum operating speed marked on the wheel. - **Set the work rest close.** OSHA sets a maximum opening of one eighth of an inch between rest and wheel, to stop work being dragged into the gap. The Army manual says one sixteenth to one eighth. The adjustable tongue guard at the top must never sit more than one quarter of an inch from the wheel. - **Keep the guards.** OSHA's exposure figures put the open arc of a bench or floor stand wheel at not more than 90 degrees, one quarter of the periphery, and a portable grinder at not more than 180 degrees with the top half of the wheel enclosed at all times. - **Never grind on the flat side of a wheel**, which weakens it and can break it, and never clamp a hand-held grinder in a vice. ### Heat: the failure you cannot undo This is the one that ruins tools permanently, and it is silent while it happens. Tool steel is hard because it was **hardened**, heated and quenched, and then **tempered**, reheated to a lower temperature to take the brittleness out. Tempering is a one-way trade: the higher the tempering temperature, the softer the steel becomes. That is the whole mechanism. A grinding wheel puts heat into a thin edge faster than the mass of the tool can carry it away, and the edge tempers itself further, in seconds, with nobody deciding to do it. **You cannot put it back by cooling it down.** The steel is permanently softer, and it will not hold an edge again until the softened metal is ground away. **The colour tells you.** Heat grows an oxide film on bright steel, and the film changes colour as it thickens. The colour these two manuals name, and the only one you need, is **blue**. The Army machine tool manual, on grinding a drill: overheating turns the drill edges blue, which indicates the drill's temper has been lost, and **the blue area must be ground completely away** to get back to sound steel. The Forest Service ax manual: you can always tell when the temper is drawn because the colour of the steel at the edge turns blue, and at minimum you have drawn the temper for at least three sixteenths of an inch back from the edge. So blue is not a stain to polish off. It is a map of the metal you now have to remove. The Forest Service's advice on grinders is worth quoting in substance because it is stronger than most people expect. Never use an electric high-speed dry bench grinder to sharpen an axe, because that type of grinder will almost certainly draw the temper and ruin it, and very few people have the skill to avoid it. The grinder it recommends instead is an old-style pedal grindstone kept wet by a constant application of water. Failing that, a file and a whetstone, which is how most quality axe sharpening is done today. The handtool manual is a little more permissive and gives the conditions: electric grinders reshape damaged tools quickly but improper grinding ruins both the bevel and the temper; high speeds remove metal fast, which can leave the blade weak and prone to chipping, and they let heat build in the head until the temper is destroyed and the blade can no longer hold an edge. Its instructions are to grind slowly, keep the blade cool, inspect frequently so you do not take off too much, and dip the tool in water or let it cool in open air. One trap: the Army manual warns that a drill which has already got too hot can **crack** when dipped into cold water or coolant. Do not let it get hot in the first place; cool it early and often rather than rescuing it late. ### Dust Dry grinding produces very fine airborne particles of both the metal and the wheel. The Army machine tool manual's instruction is direct: some machines have a vacuum dust collector, and when operating a grinder without one, wear an approved respirator; use coolant whenever possible, because it also controls dust. Where the material contains crystalline silica, the dust is a recognised long-term hazard rather than a nuisance. That is the case for concrete, stone and masonry, which is what the federal guidance below was written about, and it is worth assuming for a sandstone grinding wheel or a quarried natural stone until you know otherwise. NIOSH sets a recommended exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica of 0.05 milligrams per cubic metre as a time-weighted average and designates it a **potential occupational carcinogen**, with lung cancer the associated site. The listed effects are cough, shortness of breath, wheezing, decreased lung function and progressive respiratory symptoms of silicosis, with the eyes and respiratory system as target organs. The federal engineering answer for silica dust from a handheld grinder is one of two things: **water applied continuously to the wheel**, or **a shroud with vacuum dust collection**. OSHA also says not to clean up with compressed air, because it puts the dust back in the air, and to clear slurry before it dries out and becomes dust again. There is a happy coincidence here. Working a stone wet, which is what the oil or water on a sharpening stone is for anyway, is also the dust control. Keep the stone wet and you have very little to breathe. ### If you do cut yourself From the National Library of Medicine's public first aid guidance: - Wash your hands, then wash the cut thoroughly with mild soap and water. Use direct pressure to stop the bleeding. Apply an antibacterial ointment and a clean non-stick bandage. - For a puncture, rinse for 5 minutes under running water, then wash with soap. Look for objects in the wound but do not poke around, and if something is stuck in there do not pull it out. - **Call emergency services** if the bleeding is severe or will not stop, for example after 10 minutes of pressure, if the area has lost feeling or does not work properly, or if the person is otherwise seriously hurt. - **Contact a healthcare provider right away** if the wound is more than a quarter inch, 0.64 centimetre, deep, is on the face, or reaches bone, because stitches may be needed; if it was caused by a rusty object or a fishhook; if debris is stuck in it; if it shows signs of infection such as warmth, redness, throbbing, fever, swelling, a red streak spreading from the wound, or pus-like drainage; or if you have not had a tetanus shot in the last 10 years. A tetanus vaccine is generally recommended every 10 years. ### One legal note if you employ anyone Federal regulation makes each employer responsible for the safe condition of tools and equipment used by employees, **including tools and equipment furnished by the employees themselves**. A worker's own dull, mushroomed or cracked tool is still the employer's responsibility. OSHA's guidance adds the related rules: impact tools such as chisels, wedges and drift pins must be kept free of mushroomed heads, wooden handles must not be splintered, cracked saw blades must be taken out of service, and wrenches with sprung jaws must not be used. ## You own this when - You can say out loud that a dull tool takes more force, and that more force is what makes a slip dangerous. - You think of sharpening as removing metal until two surfaces meet, not as adding something to a blade. - You do not stop working a side until you can feel a burr along its entire length, and you know that no burr means not finished. - You pick the coarse stone when the edge is damaged, instead of doing four hundred more strokes on a fine one. - You know that stropping finishes an edge and never makes one. - You test with light and a fingernail, never with a fingertip along the edge. - You have never seen blue on an edge you ground, because you cooled it before it got there. - Your edges are stored where nothing hard can touch them, and you cut on wood, not on a plate. When those are true you can put a working edge on almost anything, which is one of the few skills that makes every other physical skill cheaper and safer at the same time. The underlying habit transfers well past blades: find the signal that tells you the job is actually done, trust that signal instead of elapsed effort, and stop when it appears. ## Sources Grouped by what kind of authority each one is. directing saw blades and knives away from aisle areas and other workers; employer responsibility and the prohibition on issuing unsafe hand tools; mushroomed impact tool heads, splintered wooden handles, cracked saw blades and sprung wrench jaws; eye or face protection when using a powered grinder and never clamping a hand-held grinder in a vice). https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA3080.pdf - Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor. *Control of Silica Dust in Construction: Handheld Grinders for Tasks Other Than Mortar Removal*, Fact Sheet FS-3628 (continuous water to the wheel or a shroud with vacuum dust collection as the two engineering controls; cleaning up slurry before it dries; not using compressed air to clean surfaces). https://www.osha.gov/sites/default/files/publications/OSHA_FS-3628.pdf - National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards*: Silica, crystalline (as respirable dust) (the 0.05 milligrams per cubic metre recommended exposure limit, the potential occupational carcinogen designation with lung cancer as the site, target organs, symptoms and exposure routes). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0684.html - National Library of Medicine, National Institutes of Health. MedlinePlus, *Cuts and puncture wounds* (washing and pressure; the 5 minute rinse for a puncture; the 10 minutes of pressure threshold for calling emergency services; the quarter inch, 0.64 centimetre, depth threshold and the face and bone criteria; rusty objects and fishhooks; the signs of infection; the 10 year tetanus interval). https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000043.htm ### Peer-reviewed literature - McGorry, R.W., Dowd, P.C. and Dempsey, P.G., Cutting moments and grip forces in meat cutting operations and the effect of knife sharpness, *Applied Ergonomics* 34(4):375-382, 2003 (fifteen professional meat cutters in two plants; mean and peak cutting moments by operation; mean grip force of 28.3% and peak of 72.6% of maximum voluntary contraction; sharper blades requiring significantly lower peak and mean cutting moments and grip forces than dull knives). Abstract read at PubMed, PMID 12880746. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12880746/ - McGorry, R.W., Dowd, P.C. and Dempsey, P.G., A technique for field measurement of knife sharpness, *Applied Ergonomics* 36(5):635-640, 2005 (that blade sharpness is measurable in the field rather than merely judged, and that measured cutting force tracks sharpness). Abstract read at PubMed, PMID 15904890. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15904890/ - Smith, G.A., Knife-related injuries treated in United States emergency departments, 1990-2008, *Journal of Emergency Medicine* 45(3):315-323, 2013 (an analysis of the Consumer Product Safety Commission's National Electronic Injury Surveillance System: an estimated 434,259 knife-related injuries annually, 1,190 per day, 1.56 per 1,000 population per year; 66% to fingers and thumbs; 94% lacerations; 47% pocket and utility knives and 36% kitchen knives; and the statement that knives cause more disabling injuries than any other type of hand tool). Abstract read at PubMed, PMID 23849364. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23849364/ - Roscioli, G., Taheri-Mousavi, S.M. and Tasan, C.C., How hair deforms steel, *Science* 369(6504):689-694, 2020 (a straight razor honed to a wedge of about 17 degrees with a tip radius of about 40 nanometres; blades failing by chipping through mixed-mode cracking at microstructural heterogeneities, before appreciable wear; and that individual structural constituents in the steel can be larger than the tip radius itself). Read as the authors' copy hosted by MIT. https://fisherp.mit.edu/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/689.full_.pdf ### What could not be sourced, and is labelled in the text Several things in this guide are trade practice rather than measured or specified values, and each says so where it appears: - **Bevel angles for kitchen knives, chisels and plane irons.** The figures everyone quotes, roughly 15 to 20 degrees per side for a kitchen knife and 25 to 30 degrees for a chisel, do not appear in any federal publication found for this guide. The sourced angles in the table are the axe, the hoe, the shovel and the drill. - **That a steel or ceramic rod realigns an edge rather than removing metal.** Universally stated by makers and cooks, not found as a measured claim in any authority cited here. - **Grit progressions.** The definition of a grit number as a sieve mesh count is sourced. The specific ladders people recommend are convention. - **Which cutting board material is kindest to an edge.** The general rule that a surface harder than the blade will chip the blade is just hardness, but the ranking of boards is not sourced here. - **The full temper-colour sequence.** Straw, brown and purple before blue are commonly quoted and are not in any source opened for this guide. Blue is, from two of them, and blue is the one that matters. - **Angle guides, hardpoint saws and serrated knives.** The suggestion of an angle guide or a folded card under the spine, the statement that a hardpoint handsaw is a consumable, and the method for serrations are all ordinary shop knowledge, labelled as such in the text. One further limitation is worth stating plainly rather than hiding in a footnote: **no study was found that directly compares injury rates between sharp and dull blades.** The force difference is measured, the hazard statement is the federal regulator's, and the step between them is mechanical reasoning. Nothing in this guide depends on that step being more than reasoning. ### A note on what is not cited Knife retailers, sharpening-equipment makers and woodworking publications carry a very large amount of sharpening advice, some of it excellent. None of them is an authority on an angle, a temperature, or an injury statistic, and where a number here exists only in that literature it has been left out or labelled as trade practice. Nothing in this guide rests on a vendor's claim about a product.

docs.text: # Working with Wood: Grain, Water, and Why Boards Move Wood is the most available structural material there is. It grows back, it cuts with hand tools, it is strong for its weight, and in most of the world you can get some without asking anyone's permission. That is why this guide exists before the one on steel. The decision you are actually making, almost every time, is this: **which piece of wood, for which job, and will it still be the right shape in a year?** Everything below serves that question. Species, grain, moisture and strength are not four separate topics; they are four ways of asking whether this board will hold and whether it will stay put. Where a number appears here, it comes from a government publication that measured it. The main one is the USDA Forest Products Laboratory *Wood Handbook*, which is the authority on anything made of wood and is in the public domain because it is a federal work. Every number traces to something in the Sources list at the bottom. Where a statement is a working rule rather than a measured value, it says so in the text. Two safety notes belong at the top rather than the bottom, because they are the only two things here that can seriously hurt you. **Wood dust is a potential occupational carcinogen and the exposure limit is far lower than people assume.** And **the table saw is the tool that actually injures people**, roughly twenty six thousand times a year in the United States. Both have their own section at the end. Neither is a reason not to work wood; both are reasons to set up properly before you start. ## The one fact that explains every surprise Wood is not one material. It is three, depending on which way you push it. The *Wood Handbook* calls wood **orthotropic**: it has unique and independent mechanical properties along three axes at right angles to each other. The **longitudinal** axis runs parallel to the fibres, which is what people mean by "with the grain". The **radial** axis runs across the growth rings, from the centre of the tree outward. The **tangential** axis runs across the grain but along the curve of the rings. Think of a bundle of drinking straws glued together. Along the straws it is enormously strong. Across them it is weak, and it wants to come apart between the straws rather than through them. That is very nearly the whole story. Almost every beginner surprise is this one fact arriving unannounced: - The board split when you drove a nail near the end. You loaded it across the straws, which is the direction with almost no strength. - The shelf cupped into a shallow trough. The two across-grain directions shrink by different amounts. - The joint failed even though the wood looked fine. The joint was carrying load in a weak direction, not the strong one. - The drawer that fit in August will not close in February. Wood takes on and gives up water with the seasons, forever. If you remember only one thing from this page, remember that wood is strong in one direction and weak in the other two, and that it changes size in the two weak directions. ## Along the grain versus across it Here is the size of the difference, in real numbers. All of these are from the *Wood Handbook*'s tests on clear, straight-grained samples. Strengths are in pounds per square inch, written psi. Take Douglas-fir at 12% moisture content. Squeeze it along the grain and it takes **7,230 psi** before crushing. Squeeze it across the grain and it gives way at **800 psi**. That is about **nine times** the strength in one direction compared to the other, in the same piece of wood. Pulling is even more lopsided. Compare like with like, using the handbook's green-condition figures for both directions: | Species | Pulled along the grain | Pulled across the grain | Ratio | |---|---|---|---| | Western hemlock | 13,000 psi | 290 psi | about 45 to 1 | | Western redcedar | 6,600 psi | 230 psi | about 29 to 1 | Roughly **thirty to forty five times stronger along the grain than across it**. No other common building material is anything like this one-sided. Steel does not care which way you pull it. This is why the across-grain numbers are the ones that decide your design. Wood almost never fails by being crushed along the grain. It fails by splitting, and splitting is tension across the grain, which is the weakest thing wood does. The other weak direction worth naming is **shear parallel to the grain**: sliding the straws past each other lengthwise. Douglas-fir manages 1,130 psi there, against 7,230 psi in compression along the grain. A joint that relies on a short shoulder of wood resisting a lengthwise sliding force is relying on one of the small numbers. ## Water: the other half of the subject A living tree is mostly water. What happens to that water on the way to your workbench governs strength, size, shape and rot. Water sits in wood in two places: **free water** in the hollow cell cavities, and **bound water** held inside the cell walls themselves. They behave completely differently, and the boundary between them is the single most useful idea in the topic. ### The fibre saturation point When all the free water has gone but the cell walls are still fully saturated, wood is at its **fibre saturation point**. The handbook is careful to say this is easier to define than to measure, but that practically it is the moisture content below which wood's physical and mechanical properties start to change, and that this **averages about 30% moisture content**, varying by a few points between species and individual pieces. Above that point, drying does nothing except remove water. The board does not shrink and it does not get stronger. Below that point, everything starts happening at once: it shrinks, it stiffens, it gets stronger, and it stops being food for fungi. Moisture content, by the way, is expressed as a percentage of the wood's *dry* weight, which is why it can exceed 100%. Green western redcedar sapwood averages **249% moisture content**: two and a half times its own dry weight in water. ### Green, air-dried, kiln-dried | Condition | Roughly what moisture content | What it means for you | |---|---|---| | Green | Douglas-fir heartwood 37%, western hemlock heartwood 85%, red alder sapwood 97%, western redcedar sapwood 249% | Full size, weakest, will shrink a lot, will rot if it stays this way | | Air-dried | Air drying is normally taken down to **20% to 25%** before anything else happens to the wood | Past the fibre saturation point, so most shrinkage has happened; below the rot threshold; still wetter than an indoor room | | Kiln-dried | Driven to the target for the end use, commonly around 8% for interior work | Stable enough for furniture and trim; stronger; costs energy, which is why mills air dry first | The green moisture figures above are species averages from the handbook, and variation between trees, and even between boards from one tree, is considerable. The handbook's recommended moisture contents at the moment you install the wood are worth knowing, because they are the target you are actually aiming at: | Use | Most of the United States | Damp coastal areas | |---|---|---| | Interior woodwork, flooring, furniture, trim | 8% average, 6% to 10% for individual pieces | 11% average, 8% to 13% | | Exterior siding, trim, sheathing | 12% average, 9% to 14% | 12% average, 9% to 14% | The handbook gives a third column for the dry southwestern states, where the interior figure drops to 6%. If you are not in the damp coastal strip or the desert southwest, the first column is yours. ### Equilibrium moisture content, and why wood never settles down Dry wood does not stay at whatever number the kiln left it at. It moves toward balance with the air around it. That balance point is the **equilibrium moisture content**, and it depends on relative humidity and temperature. At about 70 degrees Fahrenheit: | Relative humidity | Wood settles at | |---|---| | 30% | 6.2% | | 50% | 9.2% | | 65% | 12.0% | | 80% | 16.0% | | 90% | 20.5% | This is not a one-time adjustment. It is permanent, seasonal breathing. The handbook's outdoor figures for Seattle run from **12.0% in July to 16.9% in December**; Portland, Oregon runs from **11.2% to 17.2%**. Wood left outside in the Pacific Northwest swings about five percentage points of moisture content every single year, and it changes size every single year to match. Finishes do not stop this. The handbook is explicit: moisture content changes **can be retarded, but not prevented**, by protective coatings such as varnish, lacquer or paint. A finish slows the swing and evens it out. Nothing seals wood permanently. Design for movement instead of trying to prevent it. ### Dry wood is stronger wood Most of wood's mechanical properties improve as it dries below the fibre saturation point. Douglas-fir again, green against 12%: | Property | Green | At 12% moisture | |---|---|---| | Bending strength | 7,700 psi | 12,400 psi | | Crushing strength along the grain | 3,780 psi | 7,230 psi | Drying nearly doubles the crushing strength. This is a large effect and it is the main reason lumber is dried at all, alongside stability and rot resistance. ## Shrinkage, and why a board cups Wood shrinks **most tangentially, about half as much radially, and only slightly along the grain**. Those three numbers, and specifically the ratio between the first two, explain warp. Shrinkage from green to bone dry, as a percentage of the green dimension: | Species | Radial | Tangential | Tangential divided by radial | |---|---|---|---| | Western redcedar | 2.4% | 5.0% | 2.1 | | Bigleaf maple | 3.7% | 7.1% | 1.9 | | Western hemlock | 4.2% | 7.8% | 1.9 | | Red alder | 4.4% | 7.3% | 1.7 | | Douglas-fir (Coast) | 4.8% | 7.6% | 1.6 | Along the grain, shrinkage is only **0.1% to 0.2%** for most species, which is why a stud stays the length it was cut. Now picture a flatsawn board, the ordinary kind with the growth rings running roughly parallel to the face. The ring curvature means the face nearer the bark is closer to tangential, and the face nearer the pith is closer to radial. The tangential face shrinks nearly twice as much. The board becomes a shallow trough. **That is cupping, and it is simply the tangential-to-radial ratio made visible.** Nothing was done wrong. The handbook names six kinds of warp: bow, crook, twist, oval, diamond and cup. It traces all of them to one of two causes: **differences between radial, tangential and longitudinal shrinkage**, or **growth stresses** locked into the tree. Warp is made worse by irregular or distorted grain, and by two kinds of abnormal wood covered further down. Quartersawn boards, where the rings run roughly edge to edge through the thickness, move mainly in thickness rather than width and cup far less. That is the entire argument for quartersawn stock, and it costs more because you get less of it from a log. ### Working out how much it will move For the ordinary indoor range of 6% to 14% moisture content, the handbook gives a **dimensional change coefficient** for each species and direction. Multiply the starting dimension by the coefficient, then by the change in moisture content in percentage points. | Species | Radial coefficient | Tangential coefficient | |---|---|---| | Western redcedar | 0.00111 | 0.00234 | | Bigleaf maple | 0.00126 | 0.00248 | | Red alder | 0.00151 | 0.00256 | | Western hemlock | 0.00144 | 0.00274 | | Douglas-fir (Coast) | 0.00165 | 0.00267 | Worked example. You have a 12 inch wide flatsawn Douglas-fir board at 12% moisture content, and it is going into a heated house that will pull it down to 6%. Tangential, so use 0.00267. Twelve inches, times 0.00267, times six points of moisture change, gives **0.19 inches**, call it three sixteenths of an inch. The board will lose nearly a quarter inch of width. The same board quartersawn uses the radial coefficient of 0.00165 and loses **0.12 inches**, about an eighth. Same wood, same conditions, nearly half the movement. Three sixteenths of an inch is the difference between a tabletop that looks fine and one that splits because you screwed it down at both edges. This calculation takes thirty seconds and prevents a whole category of failure. ## Softwood and hardwood are botany, not hardness The names are misleading and the handbook says so directly. **Softwoods** are woods from gymnosperms, mostly conifers: pine, spruce, fir, cedar, hemlock, Douglas-fir. **Hardwoods** are woods from angiosperms, the flowering broadleaf trees: maple, oak, alder, birch, poplar. That is the entire distinction. It is about how the tree reproduces, not about how hard the wood is. The handbook's own counterexample is blunt: softwoods such as longleaf pine and Douglas-fir are typically harder than the hardwoods basswood and aspen. The measured hardness figures back it up: | Species | Type | Side hardness at 12% moisture | |---|---|---| | Douglas-fir (Coast) | Softwood | 710 lb | | American basswood | Hardwood | 410 lb | | Quaking aspen | Hardwood | 350 lb | Douglas-fir, a softwood, is twice as hard as quaking aspen and well over one and a half times as hard as basswood, both of which are hardwoods. Balsa, the lightest wood most people have ever handled, is also botanically a hardwood. So do not choose wood by the category name. Choose it by the numbers in the next section. ## The species table Everything here is from the *Wood Handbook* at 12% moisture content, tested on clear, straight-grained samples. Specific gravity is the handbook's density index, based on the wood's oven-dry weight and its volume at 12% moisture; multiplying it by 62.4 gives a rough weight in pounds per cubic foot, close enough to compare species by. Decay class is for **heartwood only**, which matters a great deal and is explained in the next section. | Species | Specific gravity | Bending strength (psi) | Stiffness (million psi) | Crushing along grain (psi) | Hardness (lb) | Shrink radial / tangential | Heartwood decay class | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Douglas-fir** (Coast) | 0.48 | 12,400 | 1.95 | 7,230 | 710 | 4.8% / 7.6% | Moderately resistant | | **Western hemlock** | 0.45 | 11,300 | 1.63 | 7,200 | 540 | 4.2% / 7.8% | Slightly or nonresistant | | **Western redcedar** | 0.32 | 7,500 | 1.11 | 4,560 | 350 | 2.4% / 5.0% | Resistant | | **Red alder** | 0.41 | 9,800 | 1.38 | 5,820 | 590 | 4.4% / 7.3% | Slightly or nonresistant | | **Bigleaf maple** | 0.48 | 10,700 | 1.45 | 5,950 | 850 | 3.7% / 7.1% | Slightly or nonresistant | | **Loblolly pine** (Southern Pine) | 0.51 | 12,800 | 1.79 | 7,130 | 690 | 4.8% / 7.4% | Slightly or nonresistant | How to read that table for a real job: - **Framing and anything structural.** Douglas-fir and Southern Pine are at the top for bending strength and stiffness, which is exactly why they are the framing lumber of the western and southern United States respectively. Western hemlock is close behind and often sold mixed with Douglas-fir. - **Anything outdoors and unpainted.** Western redcedar, and it is not close. It is the weakest and softest wood in the table by a wide margin, and it is the only one whose heartwood is rated resistant. It also has by far the least shrinkage, so it stays flat. Fence boards, siding, shingles, raised beds. - **Furniture and cabinets.** Bigleaf maple is the hardest here and takes wear well. Red alder is the classic Pacific Northwest cabinet wood: moderate in everything, easy to work, easy to finish, cheap locally. - **Anything that will get wet and is not cedar.** Nothing in the slightly or nonresistant row belongs outdoors untreated. Hemlock, alder, maple and pine all need either preservative treatment or a design that keeps them dry. ## What actually rots wood Rot is not caused by rain, or by age, or by wood being outdoors. It is caused by **fungi eating the wood**, and fungi have requirements. Take away any one of them and rot does not happen. The *Wood Handbook* is precise about this, and the numbers are more forgiving than most people expect: - **Moisture.** Serious decay occurs only when moisture content is **above the fibre saturation point, average 30%**. Below that, the growth of decay fungi is substantially arrested. - **Not from humid air alone.** By itself, water vapour in humid air will not wet wood enough to support significant decay. It takes liquid water: rain, condensation, a leak, or contact with wet ground. Humid air can still grow surface mould, which is a different and much less serious thing. - **A working safety margin of 20%.** Fully air-dried wood usually sits at no more than 20% moisture content, and the handbook treats that as a reasonable margin against fungal damage. Twenty percent is the number used in field inspections as the maximum allowable level. - **Temperature.** Decay is relatively slow below 50 degrees Fahrenheit and above 95, and essentially ceases at 35 degrees or at 100. - **Air.** Wood can be too wet to rot. Water-soaked wood does not supply enough air to the interior for typical decay fungi, which is why foundation piles below the water table and logs stored under water sprays survive indefinitely. Put together: **wood will not decay if it is kept air dry, and decay already present will not progress.** That single sentence is the whole of rot prevention. Detailing that sheds water and lets wood dry out between wettings beats any wood species and any finish. ### Heartwood versus sapwood **Heartwood** is the darker wood toward the centre of the trunk, no longer conducting sap. **Sapwood** is the lighter band nearer the bark, still alive and still moving water and sugars in the living tree. Decay resistance lives in the heartwood, because that is where the tree deposits the extractive chemicals that make certain species durable. The handbook notes that for many species the **sapwood of wood products is more susceptible to decay than the heartwood** is. This has a hard practical consequence. **A cedar board with a pale stripe of sapwood along one edge is not a decay-resistant board.** The rating in the table above applies to the dark heartwood and to nothing else. When you buy cedar for ground contact or for anything that stays wet, you are buying heartwood, and you should be able to see that you got it. The handbook's own guidance on what each class is good for: - **Very resistant** heartwood, which includes black locust, Osage-orange, red mulberry and Pacific yew, generally performs satisfactorily even **in contact with the ground**. - **Resistant** heartwood, which includes western redcedar, generally performs satisfactorily **above ground**. - The **moderately resistant** and **slightly or nonresistant** classes will usually require some form of preservative treatment. Note where Douglas-fir lands: moderately resistant, which means a Douglas-fir post in the ground is a treated post or a temporary one. Also note that old growth and second growth are not the same product. The handbook rates baldcypress and redwood differently depending on which they are, and says generally that wood from naturally resistant species grown in old growth forests is often more resistant than the same species from younger trees. ## Fasteners and joints, in terms of what the wood can carry A fastener does not hold anything. The **wood around the fastener** holds it, and it holds according to the rules above. ### Density does most of the work The handbook's equation for how hard you must pull to withdraw a nail driven into side grain is: > maximum load (lb) = 7,850 times G to the power 2.5, times nail > diameter, times depth of penetration, both in inches where G is the specific gravity of the wood. The thing to notice is the **exponent of 2.5 on density**. Holding power does not scale with density, it scales much faster. Work it through with the table above. Douglas-fir at 0.48 against western redcedar at 0.32 is only a 1.5 times difference in density, but raised to the 2.5 power it becomes **about 2.8 times the withdrawal resistance** for the same nail driven to the same depth. This is arithmetic from the handbook's own equation rather than a separate measurement, but the equation is theirs. That is the real reason cedar fence boards need more or larger fasteners than the framing behind them, and why soft woods reward ring-shank or screw-threaded fasteners that do not rely on friction alone. ### End grain barely holds at all Driving into end grain means driving parallel to the straws, and the fastener has nothing to bite between. The handbook's figures: | Fastener and direction | Compared to side grain | |---|---| | Nails, resistance to sideways load, into end grain | About **two thirds**, with minimum results near 75% | | Screws, withdrawal, into end grain | Averages **75%**, and is erratic | | Lag screws into end grain | The handbook says plainly they **should not be used** there | If a joint's strength depends on a fastener gripping end grain, redesign the joint. This is why traditional joinery uses mortises, tenons, dovetails and pegs: they transfer load into side grain and into mechanical interlock, rather than asking end grain to hold a screw. ### Moisture cycling loosens everything Nails driven into green wood that is then allowed to dry, or into dry wood that is then cycled wet and dry, **lose a major part of their holding power**. The handbook puts it as low as **25% of the value measured just after driving**. Wood shrank away from the nail, and the friction that was holding it is gone. This is the mechanism behind every loose deck board and squeaky floor you have ever met, and it is the practical reason to fasten wood at roughly the moisture content it will live at. ### Splitting, holes and spacing Splitting is tension across the grain, the weakest thing wood does, and a fastener is a wedge. Three defences, all from the handbook: - **Drill lead holes.** A hole about **90% of the nail shank diameter** gives somewhat *greater* withdrawal resistance than no hole at all, and prevents or reduces splitting, particularly in dense species. You lose nothing and gain twice. - **Keep away from edges and ends.** As a general rule, drive nails no closer to the edge of the side member than half its thickness, and no closer to the end than the full thickness of the piece. - **Use a smaller fastener.** Smaller nails can go closer to edges and ends precisely because they are less likely to split the wood. ### Metal choice Where moisture is present, certain metals in contact with wood extractives produce black staining, and certain preservative treatments corrode fasteners. The handbook's answer for staining is **stainless steel, aluminium or hot-dipped galvanised** fasteners. For wood treated with copper-based preservatives, it reports that **copper, silicon bronze and 300 series stainless steels** have performed well. ## Picking a board at the pile You now have everything needed to judge a board in about ten seconds. Look at the end grain first, then sight down the length, then look at the face. **Read the end grain.** The curve of the growth rings tells you whether the board is flatsawn, quartersawn, or in between, and therefore how much it will move and which way it will cup. Rings running roughly parallel to the wide face means flatsawn and maximum movement. Rings running roughly perpendicular to the wide face means quartersawn and about half as much. **Check the grain slope.** Grain that runs off the edge of a board rather than along it costs real strength, and the handbook quantifies it as a percentage of the same board with straight grain: | Grain slope | Bending strength | Impact resistance | Crushing along grain | |---|---|---|---| | Straight | 100% | 100% | 100% | | 1 in 20 | 93% | 90% | 100% | | 1 in 15 | 89% | 81% | 100% | | 1 in 10 | 81% | 62% | 99% | | 1 in 5 | 55% | 36% | 93% | A slope of 1 in 10, which is easy to miss and looks like nothing, removes nearly a fifth of the bending strength and **more than a third of the impact resistance**. Notice also that crushing strength along the grain barely cares. Grain slope matters enormously for anything that bends or takes a blow, and hardly at all for a post in compression. **Judge knots by where they are, not just by size.** Knots lower most mechanical properties for four reasons the handbook lists: clear wood is displaced, the fibres around the knot are distorted into cross grain, the discontinuity concentrates stress, and checks often form around knots during drying. Two things about knots surprise people: - Knots have **a much greater effect in tension than in compression**, with bending in between. In a simply supported beam the loaded face is in compression and the underside is in tension, so **a knot on the underside matters far more than the same knot on top.** If a knotty board must be a beam, put the worst knot on the upper face. - **Encased knots**, the dead loose ones that fall out and leave a hole, tend to come with *less* cross grain than tight intergrown knots, and the handbook rates them as generally **less problematic for most mechanical properties**. They look worse and are often structurally kinder. You may still reject one for appearance, or because a hole is a hole, but do not assume a tight knot is automatically the stronger board. **Sight down the length for warp.** Bow, crook, twist and cup all show up in a two second sight down the edge and the face. A twisted board is the one to leave behind; the other three can often be worked around. **Reject reaction wood and juvenile wood.** Normal wood shrinks 0.1% to 0.2% along its length. Reaction wood, which forms in leaning trunks and under branches, and juvenile wood from near the centre of the tree, **can shrink 2% lengthwise**, ten to twenty times as much. That is what makes a stud crook weeks after it is nailed in. Look for wood from very near the pith, unusually wide and uneven growth rings, and an abnormally dense, dull-looking zone on one side of the board. **Check for surface checks**, the fine splits that open on the face. They form early in drying when the outer shell is stressed in tension enough to fracture, and they are most common **on the face of flatsawn boards**. **Buy wood at the moisture content it will live at.** A kiln-dried board that has spent three weeks on an open rack in a wet Pacific Northwest winter is not a kiln-dried board any more. If it matters, bring the wood inside and let it sit in the room it will live in for a couple of weeks before you cut joinery. This is common trade practice rather than a measured recommendation, but the equilibrium moisture content figures above are exactly why it works. ## Safety ### Wood dust This is the hazard people take least seriously and should take most seriously, because it accumulates over years and there is no moment when it hurts. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health classifies **wood dust as a potential occupational carcinogen**, with the cancer site given as **nasal cancer**. Its recommended exposure limit is a time-weighted average of **1 milligram per cubic metre**. The OSHA permissible limit is much higher, at 15 milligrams per cubic metre total dust and 5 milligrams per cubic metre respirable, so the two disagree by more than a factor of ten and the NIOSH figure is the health-based one. The non-cancer effects listed are eye irritation, nosebleeds, dermatitis, respiratory hypersensitivity, granulomatous pneumonitis, asthma, cough, wheezing, sinusitis and prolonged colds. The target organs are the eyes, skin and respiratory system, and the exposure routes include skin and eye contact as well as breathing it. One detail matters especially in the Pacific Northwest: **western red cedar dust is the same NIOSH entry as wood dust**, sharing its identifier. The wood most worth building with outdoors here is also on the respiratory hazard list. What this means in practice: dust collection at the tool, not a broom afterwards; a properly fitted respirator rather than a paper nuisance mask for sanding and routing; and not eating lunch in a shop full of airborne dust. A sanding session generates far more respirable dust than a sawing session, and produces almost no visible mess, which is exactly backwards from how people judge risk. ### The tools that actually injure people The table saw is the one. The Consumer Product Safety Commission estimated that in 2017 there were **26,500 table saw blade-contact injuries treated in United States emergency departments**. Of those, **25,600, or 96.4%, involved a finger**. The breakdown by diagnosis was **16,100 lacerations, 5,500 fractures, and 2,800 amputations**. Two thousand eight hundred amputations in one year, from one tool. A common belief is that kickback causes most of these. The Commission's assessment of its own incident data is that **most blade-contact injuries are not related to kickback**. Contact happens when a hand gets too close feeding a small workpiece, when the operator is distracted, when a glove catches the blade, when someone reaches to regain control of a workpiece, and when someone brushes debris off the table while the blade is still coasting after shutoff. Federal workplace regulation requires three specific devices on a hand-fed circular ripsaw, and they are worth naming because home saws are frequently run without them: 1. **A hood** completely enclosing the portion of the saw above the table and above the material, self-adjusting to the thickness of the work. 2. **A spreader**, made of hard tempered steel and thinner than the saw kerf, to prevent material from squeezing the saw or being thrown back at the operator. This is the riving knife. The regulation permits its removal for grooving, dadoing and rabbeting, and requires that it be **immediately replaced** when those operations are finished. 3. **Nonkickback fingers or dogs**, positioned to oppose the saw's tendency to pick up the material and throw it back. The same regulation requires a power control the operator can reach **without leaving the point of operation**, which is worth arranging even in a home shop. Two other machines deserve a mention because they injure differently: - **The jointer.** The regulation requires a cylindrical cutting head with the knife projecting **no more than one eighth of an inch** beyond the body of the head, an automatic guard covering the head on the working side of the fence, and a guard covering the head behind the fence. A jointer has no blade guard you can see working and the cutter is directly under your hands. Push blocks are not optional. - **The portable circular saw.** Regulation requires both an upper and a lower guard covering the saw to the depth of the teeth, with the lower guard returning **automatically and instantly** to the covering position when the tool is withdrawn from the work, plus a constant-pressure switch that cuts power when released. A sticky lower guard on a well-used saw is a genuine defect, not a quirk. None of this replaces learning the tools from someone who knows them. It does tell you what "set up correctly" looks like, and it tells you which guard someone removed. ## You own this when - You can say which of the three directions a load is acting in, and whether that is the strong one or one of the weak ones. - You can look at the end of a board and say whether it will cup, and roughly how much it will move across its width between summer and winter. - You know that 30% moisture content is where shrinkage and rot both begin, and that 20% is the working margin below it. - You buy heartwood when you buy for decay resistance, and you can see the difference in the board. - You do not ask end grain to hold a screw. - You have dust collection running before the tool starts, and the spreader is back on the saw before the next rip cut. When those are true you can walk into any pile of lumber, in any country, and choose correctly for the job. The underlying skill transfers well beyond wood: knowing which direction a material is strong in, knowing what environmental variable it responds to, and knowing which failure mode is the one that actually hurts someone are the same three questions behind every material you will ever build with. ## Sources Every source below is a work of the United States federal government and is therefore in the public domain, so all of it can be redistributed with this guide. That is unusual and it is why this topic could be written entirely from primary authorities: there was no need to cite a retailer, a trade association or a woodworking publication for anything. ### United States government (public domain) - USDA Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory. *Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material*, General Technical Report FPL-GTR-282, 2021. Chapter 4, Moisture Relations and Physical Properties of Wood (fibre saturation point, equilibrium moisture content, green moisture content by species, shrinkage values, longitudinal shrinkage, anisotropic dimensional behaviour); Chapter 5, Mechanical Properties of Wood (the orthotropic axes, strength properties by species, tension parallel to grain, grain slope, knots, effect of moisture content on strength, hardwood and softwood definitions); Chapter 8, Fastenings (nail withdrawal equation, end grain penalties, moisture cycling, lead holes, spacing, fastener metals); Chapter 13, Drying and Control of Moisture Content and Dimensional Changes (air drying and kiln drying, recommended moisture content at installation, outdoor equilibrium moisture content by city, dimensional change coefficients, warp, surface checks); Chapter 14, Biodeterioration of Wood (heartwood decay resistance groupings). https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/fplgtr/fplgtr282/fpl_gtr282.pdf - USDA Forest Service, Forest Products Laboratory. *Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material*, General Technical Report FPL-GTR-190, 2010. Chapter 14, Biodeterioration of Wood (the conditions decay fungi require: moisture above fibre saturation, the 20% air-dry margin, the temperature range, why water-soaked wood does not decay, and sapwood being more susceptible than heartwood in wood products). An earlier edition of the handbook above, cited where it states these conditions more completely. https://www.fpl.fs.usda.gov/documnts/fplgtr/fplgtr190/chapter_14.pdf - National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. *NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards*: Wood dust, which is also the entry for western red cedar dust (recommended exposure limit, potential occupational carcinogen designation, nasal cancer site, OSHA permissible limit, symptoms, target organs, exposure routes). https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/npg/npgd0667.html - Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor. 29 CFR 1910.213, Woodworking machinery requirements (ripsaw hood, spreader and nonkickback fingers; the power control at the point of operation; jointer cutting head knife projection and guarding). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol5-sec1910-213.xml - Occupational Safety and Health Administration, US Department of Labor. 29 CFR 1910.243, Guarding of portable powered tools (portable circular saw upper and lower guards, automatic guard return, constant-pressure switch). https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/CFR-2024-title29-vol5/xml/CFR-2024-title29-vol5-sec1910-243.xml - Consumer Product Safety Commission. *Safety Standard Addressing Blade-Contact Injuries on Table Saws*, supplemental notice of proposed rulemaking, Federal Register, 1 November 2023 (the 2017 Special Study estimates of emergency-department-treated table saw blade-contact injuries, the share involving fingers, the diagnosis breakdown, and the Commission's assessment that most blade-contact injuries are not kickback-related). Cited for the injury data, not for the rule, which was a proposal. https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/11/01/2023-23898/safety-standard-addressing-blade-contact-injuries-on-table-saws ### A note on what is not cited Lumber retailers, tool manufacturers and woodworking publications carry a great deal of wood advice, some of it good. None of it is an authority on a measured property, and where their numbers disagree with the *Wood Handbook*, the handbook measured it and they did not. Nothing in this guide rests on one.
